News.title: Prince William's 'troubled' teenage years were worlds away from those Prince George faces
News.content:
On the eve of his teenage years officially beginning, Prince George’s future has many similarities to that of his father, Prince William.

In September, George will follow in his father’s footsteps by starting at his new school, Eton College, while, like William before him, he is also being gradually introduced to more and more royal duties. But for the Prince of Wales, his life at 13 couldn’t have been more different to that of his eldest son, who becomes a teenager tomorrow.

Back in June 1995, William turned 13 at the height of his own parents’ bitter split, which played out in public. It came just weeks before he started at Eton College as he and brother Prince Harry shuttled between living with mum, Princess Diana and their dad, then Prince Charles.

5 View 5 Images Prince George who turns 13 today (Image: WireImage) 5 View 5 Images Prince William back when he was 13 in 1995 (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

‌



Former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond recalled having a long chat during a meeting with the late Diana at Kensington Palace the exact month William turned 13.

The royal expert said the princess confided in her that at that time, the burden of future Kingship weighed heavily on William’s shoulders - although he was slowly coming to terms with his future role.

However, she told the Mirror: “At this time in his life, William was troubled by a great deal more than just his destiny. He had witnessed and lived through the brutal breakup of his parents’ marriage; he had supported his mother through her distress, anger, and sadness.

“He and Harry had become used to a rather nomadic life: sometimes with their father, sometimes with their mother and much of the time at school.

‌



View 5 Images William shortly before his 13th birthday with his parents the now King Charles and the late Princess Diana (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

“Their parents’ private lives had become public. His father had admitted adultery on national television, and there was worse to come. It was only a few months after William’s 13th birthday, during his first term at Eton, that Diana recorded her now notorious Panorama interview in which she, too, admitted adultery and poured out her heart about her life and marriage. William was mortified.”

Now, William has put family life at the heart of everything he does, and today George is growing up in a more stable household away from the public spotlight - and having as normal an upbringing as possible while he gains a deeper understanding of his future duties.

And Jennie explained: “George may well feel the burden of Kingship on his shoulders, but he has two united and highly supportive parents who have always encouraged him to discuss his feelings and fears.

‌



“He has been brought up in a stable, loving household – not sent away to boarding school at the age of eight – with parents who have consciously and unashamedly put their children before their work at important times in their lives and during school holidays.

View 5 Images William with his late mother and younger brother, Prince Harry in the months after turning 13 (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

“Of course, George and his siblings have had the trauma of their mother’s shock diagnosis of cancer and the treatment which followed, which is a terrible thing for any young boy to cope with. But George has had his father at his side.”

The dawn of his teenage years will see huge changes for George as his new school, which he will enrol in September, will see him board full-time for the first time.

‌



Not only will it be a significant step for the future King, it will also be a big change for his parents and his siblings, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, who all attended Lambrook School together.

But Jennie said: “William - and Catherine - are bound to worry about their little boy as he becomes a teenager and sets off for boarding school. It’s a huge step and a big change in any family.

View 5 Images A 13-year-old William on his first day at Eton in September 1995 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“But William knows exactly what life is like at Eton and he knows exactly what it’s like to be an heir to the throne. There is no one better placed to help and guide George through his teenage years.

“Diana told me the country was lucky to have William. I think George is exceptionally lucky to have the parents he has. They have given him the best, most secure start in life: he knows how much they love one another and how much they love him. He looks like a young man well equipped for this next chapter.”

News.title: Andy Burnham live: New Prime Minister sets challenge to ministers during his first Cabinet meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham has thrown down the gauntlet, asking MPs to "take that little bit of pressure off people's shoulders" as he sets sights to help ease families facing the cost-of-living crisis

Andy Burnham today chaired his first Cabinet meeting and told his appointed ministers to examine “all possible ways” to help families struggling with high costs.

In a challenge to his top team one their applause had died down, the new Prime Minister said their task was to "take that little bit of pressure off people's shoulders" and show them help was coming so they could have some hope things were improving.

He told the meeting: "That’s the mission that we’ve got to set ourselves together” and asked his colleagues to look into what their department could do to ease cost-of-living pressures, “big and small,” saying: “We need to be a cost-of-living Government, getting that cost of living down, looking at all possible ways of doing that.”

Burnham started today by making good on his promise for “breathing space” for struggling households, a key plinth of his economic plans unveiled in his maiden speech outside No 10 on Monday. The move will see VAT removed from domestic electricity bills from October 1.

Burnham said: “Westminster has not been working for people for too long, with families struggling with the cost of living. That needs to change. I said I wanted to give people breathing space, and that’s what I’m announcing on my second day as Prime Minister. We’re taking immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people’s pockets and bring back hope.”

It is estimated that the change will reduce the annual Ofgem price cap by around £45 from October, with companies expected to pass the reduction onto customers.

Chancellor John Healey said: “For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living. Today’s energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills, and provide some reassurance this winter". He continued: “This measure is funded this year from cancelling the Digital ID programme, and it will help bring down inflation while supporting households in every postcode.”

The fully priced plan from Mr Healey comes as Burnham continues to pad out his cabinet, with a number of key appointments made since yesterday, including Ed Miliband receiving the FCDO brief, Angela Rayner returning as Housing Secretary, and Shabana Mahmood staying on as Home Secretary.

News.title: Armed police swarm Surrey school after 'weapon' panic as two teens arrested
News.content:
Armed police swarm Surrey school after 'weapon' panic as two teens arrested

Three Rivers Academy, Three Rivers Primary School and Toad Hall Nursery placed themselves into lockdown after reports of a person armed with a weapon

View Image Police rushed to Three Rivers Academy in Hersham (Image: GoogleMaps)

Three schools in Surrey were locked down after a person was allegedly seen armed with a weapon near the premises.

Police, including armed officers, were called to Bell Farm Way in Hersham at 3pm today, with road closures also put in place. Three Rivers Academy, and nearby Three Rivers Primary School and Toad Hall Nursery all placed themselves into lockdown due to the reports.

Three Rivers Academy instigated a temporary lockdown procedure as a precaution to safeguard staff and students. A statement on the school's website at the time of the lockdown read: "We are currently in lockdown by instruction from the police due to an outside incident. All students inside school are safe."

The lockdown has now been lifted and all students have been allowed to go home. Lockdown conditions at Three Rivers Primary School and Toad Hall Nursery have also been lifted and staff and children have left both sites, Surrey Police said.

Officers were on scene within eight minutes of the 999 call and two 18-year-old men were arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon. Both suspects remain in police custody.

Article continues below

Elmbridge Borough Commander Inspector Chris Thoday said: "We take any report of this nature extremely seriously and had officers at the scene within minutes.

"The school and other education facilities nearby also quickly instigated their well-prepared safeguarding plans to ensure the safety of pupils and staff. We fully understand how concerning incidents like this are for our community and our investigation into the circumstances continues.

"Anyone with information which could assist us is asked to contact police if they have not already been spoken to."

News.title: Keir Starmer goes down the pub with Rachel Reeves after stepping down as Prime Minister
News.content:
Keir Starmer goes down the pub with Rachel Reeves after stepping down as Prime Minister

Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves entered Parliament with a massive majority, but just a couple of years into the job, both left Downing Street and headed straight to the pub

View 5 Images Keir Starmer left Downing Street after being elected with a massive majority in 2024 (Image: n.c)

Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves were spotted at a pub with drinks in hand just hours they left Downing Street.

‌



The former Prime Minister and Chancellor rocked up to The Pineapple pub in Kentish Town, north London, while Ex-Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham put together his Cabinet. Rather than appearing downtrodden, photographs published today showed the pair in seemingly good spirits.

‌



Mr Starmer was seen chatting and texting on the phone while holding a pint in his hand after he arrived. Another snap at the pub showed the dad of two leaning by the door after putting his pint down and speaking to someone on the phone.

‌



View 5 Images Keir Starmer was on the phone while sipping a pint (Image: n.c)

Andy Burnham's timetable today as he replaces Keir Starmer as Prime Minister READ MORE :

The Pineapple brands itself as northwest London's "beloved back street boozer." In addition to a selection of pints and spirits, the pub also offers Thai food, although it is unclear if any of the ex-Prime Minister's team tucked into any tasty treats.

Just hours before he left Downing Street, Mr Starmer said his "work is done." He later added: "I go with a smile and I go proud of everything that we have achieved."

‌



View 5 Images Rachel Reeves appeared in happy spirits despite leaving Downing Street (Image: n.c)

The outgoing Prime Minister said he wished Mr Burnham "every success" before exiting Downing Street, Mr Burnham is now the UK's seventh Prime Minister since 2016, an unprecedented position in Post War Britain.

At the pub, Ms Reeves was surrounded by friends and colleagues while sipping some wine. The former Chancellor was also seen being embraced by one of her aides at the pub.

‌



View 5 Images Ms Reeves declined a job offer from Mr Burnham (Image: n.c)

Ms Reeves had reportedly been offered the role of Defence Secretary, but she ultimately declined the offer. She was the first female Chancellor in British history, but her position became uncertain after it became clear Mr Burnham would become Labour Party leader and, later, Prime Minister.

Ms Reeves said on social media after leaving Downing Street: "It has been the privilege of my life to serve as the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The economy today is stronger, fairer and more resilient because of the choices we have taken as a Labour Government over the past two years."

Article continues below

View 5 Images The Pineapple pub offers Thai treats to punters (Image: n.c)

The mum of two added: "Stability restored, investment delivered and reform to our economy under way. I said when I was appointed Chancellor that I would judge my time in office if the lives ordinary working class people have been improved. I’m proud to say that they have.

"And to every young woman and girl let my time in office show there should be no ceilings on your ambitions, your hopes or your dreams. I wish the very best of luck to my successor, Andy and his cabinet. You have my full support, and I will continue to play my part in helping this Labour government deliver the change the country needs."

News.title: Woman stabbed at church as she prayed before mass in terrifying 'random' attack
News.content:
Woman stabbed at church as she prayed before mass in terrifying 'random' attack

The stabbing took place today at Holy Cross Church in Summerhill, Tramore, County Waterford, with the victim, aged in her 50s, described as a 'lovely woman'

View 3 Images Emergency services at the scene at Holy Cross Church, Tramore (WLR FM) (Image: WLR FM)

A woman has been stabbed inside a church in Ireland just before morning Mass.

‌



The attack took place today at Holy Cross Church in, Tramore, County Waterford, in Ireland at about 9.45am. The victim, aged in her 50s and named as Mary McNamara, reportedly suffered a single knife wound before she was rushed to hospital.

‌



Multiple units, including specialist armed police from the Armed Support Unit, responded to the incident along with paramedics. The victim suffered serious but not life-threatening injuries, the Gardai have said.

‌



Speaking to the Irish Mirror, local parishioner Ann O'Connor, said she was with Ms McNamara when the attack occurred and that the victim was chased by her attacker.

She said: "The lady that was stabbed was kneeling behind me so I didn't see a lot but it was very traumatic. He was there and he came down the church and stopped. He just lunged with a knife and she ran and he after her," she said.

Ms O'Connor described the woman as a "lovely person," and "very gentle".

‌



View 3 Images Police, including armed officers, rushed to the church

Armed police swarm Surrey school after 'weapon' panic as two teens arrested READ MORE :

Gardai say a man in his 30s - reportedly a white Irish national - was later arrested at a domestic residence in the area - and is currently being detained at a Garda Station in Co Waterford. Officers can hold him for up to 24 hours. Gardai also say they have seized a knife as part of the investigation.

The force said in its statement that although the woman suffered serious injuries in the attack, her life is understood to be not in danger at this stage.

‌



Parish Priest Richard O’Halloran described what had occurred as “a very shocking event.”

"However the people and indeed my colleague who was there at the time responded wonderfully well. All the emergency services were called and they looked after everything that was happening. This was an incident before Mass. It was in the main body of the church."

View 3 Images The horror incident happened at the Holy Cross Church in Tramore (Image: Google)

‌



Fr O'Halloran confirmed that the woman is a member of the parish and well known in the area. He believed the incident to be random in nature but said "that's in the hands of the guards". He said his prayers and prayers of those in the parish are with the victim.

Officers are now asking for anyone who was in the area to contact police. A Gardai statement said: "Gardaí are appealing for witnesses to come forward.

"Any person who was in the vicinity of Summerhill, Tramore between 9:15am and 10:15am on Tuesday 21st July and who may have camera footage (including dash-cam) is asked to make this footage available to Gardaí.

Article continues below

"Anyone with information is asked to contact Tramore Garda Station on (051) 391620, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda Station. Investigations are ongoing."

News.title: Ugly protests erupt after Abderrahim Fakir dies pleading 'help' while restrained by police
News.content:
Ugly protests erupt after Abderrahim Fakir dies pleading 'help' while restrained by police

Footage shared on social media - deemed by the Mirror too distressing to publish - shows two police officers sit on Abderrahim Fakir as he repeatedly calls for help

View 3 Images Demonstrations have happened in Bologna his week (Image: Nicola Marfisi/AGF/Shutterstock)

A protest erupted after the death of a man who repeatedly pleaded for help as officers restrained him on the ground.

‌



Police clashed with demonstrators in Bologna, Italy, after Abderrahim Fakir died on Sunday when officers were called following reports of a man behaving aggressively and damaging a vehicle. Local residents had alerted police shortly after midday over reports of erratic behaviour.

‌



Video shared widely across social media - too distressing for the Mirror too distressing to publish - appears to show the 42-year-old man repeatedly crying out “aiuto, aiuto, basta” (“Help, help, that’s enough”) as two officers restrain him on the ground while ambulance workers stand nearby.

‌



The Moroccan-born entrepreneur, who had lived in Italy since he was five years old, had heart problems and asthma. Footage appears to show him gradually becoming motionless as officers bound his ankles together.

View 3 Images Protests have happened in Bologna following the death (Image: Guido Calamosca/LaPresse/Shutterstock)

CCTV captures incredible moment hero teen leaps into runaway car to save two women READ MORE :

Officers reportedly called paramedics shortly after arriving and initially tried to calm Fakir before using pepper spray and restraining him while attempting to handcuff him. Police told ambulance workers he was “having a psychiatric episode”.

‌



Prosecutors have since opened an investigation into Mr Fakir’s death and requested officers’ body camera footage, while human rights campaigners and Italy’s opposition parties have demanded urgent answers.

His sister, Khadija, told the Corriere della Sera newspaper: “You can’t die like this. The police have to protect us. If someone is agitated, you have to calm them down.”

The death sparked protests across Bologna on Monday night, with thousands of demonstrators taking to the streets carrying signs reading “Justice for Fakir” and “State murders”. Some protesters threw firecrackers near police buildings, while officers responded with tear gas and water cannon. Others staged a sit-down protest in a city square holding photographs of Fakir, according to the Ansa news agency

‌



.

View 3 Images Thousands of demonstrators have gathered, with some carrying signs reading 'Justice for Fakir' (Image: Guido Calamosca/LaPresse/Shutterstock)

The incident has drawn comparisons with George Floyd’s murder in the US six years ago, while others likened the restraint tactics to those used by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) under Donald Trump.

‌



Barbara Spinelli, a lawyer, told Ansa she had met Fakir last year when he applied to renew his permit to stay. He had been “a very kind, well educated, respectful person” who was in Italy legally but worried about being expelled.

She said: “I told him: ‘We are in Italy, a democratic country. Here the police respect the rules I don’t know how I will ever again manage to tell someone they don’t need to be afraid.”

Ilaria Cucchi, a senator whose brother died in custody in 2009, told Agence France-Presse she was sickened by the “solidarity and thanks” expressed to police after such an “inhumane act”.

‌



Mr Cucchi, a member of the opposition Greens and Left alliance (AVS) party, criticised Meloni and her coalition government, saying their “policies seeped in hatred and racism” had fostered a climate of violence.

Francesco Boccia, head of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD) in the Senate, told La Repubblica: “If the right wants to import the ICE model, this is the wrong country for it. We have democratic antibodies.”

Far-right Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an investigation would be carried out into Fakir’s death “without prejudice”, but condemned the violence that broke out in the aftermath.

Article continues below

Italy’s Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Piantedosi told public television: “Whoever makes insulting remarks against the police shows they have no trust in our law enforcement nor in our justice system [and] should look into what happened.”

News.title: M25 traffic live: Major delays anticlockwise after lorry crashes into embankment
News.content:
Delays of over an hour are expected after congestion on J6 of the M25 is reported to stretch back for seven miles.

A large section of the M25 has come to a standstill after a lorry crashed into an embankment, sparking major delays with emergency services rushing to the scene.

The crash happened anticlockwise on Junction 6 at Godstone and Clacket Lane Services at around 10am this morning, resulting in the closure of two of the motorway's four lanes.

Significant queues have been building in the area, with delays of up to 60 minutes and around seven miles of congestion reported in the area.

News.title: Flights cancelled at Bordeaux Airport as huge fire breaks out with firefighters killed
News.content:
Flights cancelled at Bordeaux Airport as huge fire breaks out with firefighters killed

Two firefighters have tragically died fighting a huge blaze at Bordeaux Airport, which grounded flights and shut down nearby roads

View 2 Images Two firefighters have died while battling the ongoing vegetation fire near Bordeaux-Mérignac airport (Image: @InfosFrancaises/X)

Flights at Bordeaux Airport were cancelled after a huge fire erupted nearby which killed two firefighters tackling the blaze.

‌



French media reports that the fire broke out at a nearby building on Avenue Roland Garros, close to the airport's car park, at around 2:30pm this afternoon, before quickly spreading across about one hectare of land and sending massive plumes of black smoke into the sky.

‌



France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that two firefighters had tragically perished while attempting to extinguish the blaze. Flights from the airport are gradually resuming after being grounded but passengers have been urged to check the status of their flights before travelling. Firefighters remain at the scene.

‌



View 2 Images The blaze has not been extinguished but is thought to be under control. (Image: @InfosFrancaises/X)

French President Emmanuel Macron paid tribute to the two firefighters killed in a post on X, writing: "Two firefighters lost their lives while responding to a fire in Mérignac.

‌



"I extend to their families, to their loved ones, and to the firefighters of France the condolences, the gratitude, and the support of the Nation."

Laurent Nuñez wrote on X: "The Nation bows before their courage and their commitment to protecting the French people."

France has been gripped by a deadly heatwave in recent weeks that has resulted in wildfires, a public health crisis and more than 2,000 deaths to date.

Article continues below

Firefighters are also battling a separate blaze in the Var department in the south-east of the country.

Nearly 600 firefighters are tackling a field fire near Ponteves that has burned around 350 hectares. More than 150 people have been evacuated as a precaution from the nearby towns of Cotignac and Sillans-la-Cascade.

Authorities said six people have suffered minor smoke inhalation and some homes have been damaged.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch in an attack that was caught on camera, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man charged with her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.

Kerry, who prosecutors say was in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer in her kitchen, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off.

The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.

At the Old Bailey hearing, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the attack on Widdecombe had been carried out with a "ferocity of violence".

Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.

The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.

News.title: Burnham tells cabinet to tackle living costs at first meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to lead a "cost of living government," as he chaired his first cabinet meeting as prime minister.

He told his newly-assembled top team that he wanted to make living expenses a key priority, and give people a "sense that help is coming" on costs.

It comes after he announced a VAT cut to household energy bills from October, in his first major announcement since taking office.

But his plan to pay for the policy by scrapping Sir Keir Starmer's digital ID scheme led to an early row over whether the plan was properly funded.

Downing Street said the estimated Â£850m cost of the VAT cut over the rest of the financial year could come from Â£1.8bn earmarked by the previous government to roll out the digital ID scheme in the next three years.

But Darren Jones, who was among a clutch of Starmer loyalists sacked from the cabinet on Monday, said the ID programme was "unfunded" and Burnham would need to set out where the money would be found.

Opposition parties also seized on the announcement, pointing out the government's budget watchdog has previously said the money to fund digital ID was due to be found from within existing budgets.

"We are only one day in and already Labour are playing fast and loose with the public finances," said Conservative shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride.

The PM's spokesman insisted the policy would be funded by redirecting "savings" identified by departments to cover the cost of the ID scheme.

Burnham was given a round of applause by his senior ministers earlier, as he opened the first meeting of his new cabinet after appointing his top team on Monday evening. More junior picks are expected to follow on Tuesday.

Monday's wide-ranging reshuffle saw Starmer loyalists such as Rachel Reeves and David Lammy out of government, with Ed Miliband promoted to foreign secretary and Burnham ally Louise Haigh given a big job running the Cabinet Office.

In a move that took Westminster by surprise, John Healey, who resigned as Starmer's defence secretary in a row over military spending, has been given the crucial role of chancellor.

Speaking to staff at the Treasury, where he was a minister during the New Labour period, Healey said discipline over tax and spending would be his "first duty", as he recommitted to the tax and spending rules set by his predecessor.

But he added that government would seek to make the "fullest possible use of public investment" within the framework, alongside making the most of private and international investment.

News.title: Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM
News.content:
Shortly after Andy Burnham telephoned a number of Keir Starmer's allies to sack them from the cabinet on Monday afternoon, John Healey received the signal to head to Number 10.

Wearing a suit and one of his many red ties, the former defence secretary left parliament alone via a back entrance next to a pub.

"I'm on my way to a meeting," he said with a slight smile as he marched down Whitehall.

Healey's imminent appointment as chancellor was a surprise - to him, to his Labour colleagues, and to the British public.

It was a consequential moment among a flurry of announcements from the new prime minister, including today's cut in VAT on energy bills, that demonstrate the new government's intention to move at breakneck speed - at least for now.

The Conservatives support that tax cut but have questioned its funding.

Five weeks earlier Healey had weakened Keir Starmer's grip on Downing Street by quitting as defence secretary in a row over military spending.

Soon he would be back around the cabinet table alongside two others whose recent resignations had also damaged Starmer - new defence secretary Wes Streeting and new energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Were they rewarded for rebelling and hastening Burnham's path to office? Possibly.

But all three are also widely seen as skilled operators taking on complex roles.

News.title: Argentina's Fernandez defends team after ugly scenes in World Cup final loss to Spain
News.content:
Midfielder Enzo Fernandez has claimed Argentina represented their nation "in the best possible way" during the World Cup, despite ugly scenes during and after their final loss to Spain.

Fernandez was sent off late in normal time for two yellow cards and Spain won 1-0 after extra time on Sunday in New Jersey.

His first booking was for showing dissent towards Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic and Fernandez was later dismissed for catching Pau Cubarsi with a challenge that sent the defender cartwheeling in the air.

But, in a statement on social media, the Chelsea midfielder did not mention the red card and said: "As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result.

"For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn't just about winning; it's about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up.

"It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment."

News.title: Parts of the UK move closer to drought
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

In Wales, where just 5% of July rainfall has fallen, Natural Resources Wales has moved the worst affected regions in the north and south-east into "prolonged dry weather status", the first step in its drought plan.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

As the effects of human-induced climate change continue, the Met Office expects our summers to become hotter and drier, external in the future. In fact, by 2070, our summers could be up to 60% drier and 1-6C warmer compared to 1990.

News.title: Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for 10 million
News.content:
Thames Water has announced a hosepipe ban affecting 10.1 million customers after an "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The restrictions mean, from Thursday, hosepipes should not be used for watering gardens or allotments, cleaning cars, filling paddling pools or swimming pools, or cleaning windows.

The water company said its region had seen 40% of average rainfall, and more days at or above 34C this year than ever recorded before.

Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources, said: "We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment."

The ban applies to all customers that Thames Water supplies with drinking water and comes into effect on Thursday.

The company provides water to customers across parts of Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Surrey, the Thames Valley, Greater London, and the surrounding areas, external.

It provides water and wastewater services to 16 million customers overall.

It said water use was currently 10% above normal in the Thames Valley and Home Counties and 7% above normal in London, which amounted to an extra 100 million litres of water every day.

News.title: Ryanair boss says 'foreign object' may have caused plane window incident
News.content:
An incident on a Ryanair flight which saw a passenger partially sucked out of a plane window may have been caused by "foreign object damage" to an engine, said the airline's boss.

Michael O'Leary said an initial investigation into the incident on 10 July between Greece and Germany suggests "it looks like a foreign object damage to the engine on takeoff at Thessaloniki but ... we can't say that definitively".

He insisted that the engine on the 18-year-old Boeing 737 plane had been fully serviced and overhauled in the past two years.

Serbian national Ljubisa KaroviÄ's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the plane's window, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".

His wife Svetlana GrkoviÄ MaksimoviÄ told BBC Serbia that she and two other passengers held on to his legs for several minutes.

She said: "We pulled him back together. His entire face was deformed and blood was pouring from his nose and mouth."

He was taken to hospital after the plane made an emergency landing.

Passengers told local media they heard "some kind of explosion" on board.

The aircraft was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.

Confirmation that the damage was caused by an external object could affect Ryanair or Boeing's liabilities over the incident.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. O'Leary said that a draft report would be issued in about 28 days.

News.title: Lindt's Easter chocolate sales fall after price hike
News.content:
Lindt has partially U-turned on its decision to hike prices after Easter chocolate sales dropped.

The Swiss chocolate maker said a "necessary groupwide" price surge of 11.8% was one of the reasons revenue shrank in the first half of this year, particularly in the UK, Germany, and Switzerland.

It also blamed weaker Easter demand and a drop in tourism from Asia and the Middle East "due to geopolitical uncertainties". In response, it said it has adjusted prices and boosted marketing in certain regions for the second half of the year.

Around Easter, Lindt is known for its chocolate rabbits wrapped in gold-coloured foil and decorated with a red ribbon and bell on their necks.

Overall, the company's sales dipped 0.9%, with European sales down by 2.1%. It added that "performance was impacted by more price-sensitive and mature markets such as Germany, Switzerland and the UK".

By volume, meaning the amount of chocolate sold rather than the money it made, overall sales sank 7.5%. Pre-tax profit fell 1.5%.

Meanwhile, sales of Lindt chocolate in airports decreased "due to ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, and therefore declining passenger traffic".

Lindt said its sales picked up in North America, Australia, China, and Japan, though these countries account for a much smaller slice of its sales than Europe, where it makes over half its revenue.

Lindt chief executive Adalbert Lechner said: "The actions we have initiated focus on volume recovery in the second half of 2026 and lay the foundation to regain volume growth momentum in 2027."

Lindt is not the only chocolate firm which has been putting prices up.

Experts say climate change has led to extreme rainfall and droughts which have decreased cocoa farmers' crops.

This pushes up costs of making chocolate, and companies have chosen different ways to react to this, with some reducing chocolate content or sizes rather than raising prices.

According to the latest official data, the annual rate of chocolate and sweet price rises is 7.9%, external â much higher than the general rate of UK inflation at 2.8%, external.

News.title: Union plans rail strikes over train safety concerns
News.content:
A union that represents railway staff has announced plans for its members at East Midlands Railway (EMR) to take strike action over "growing safety concerns the company has failed to address".

The RMT union said it had been in dispute with EMR since April following the rollout of the 810 fleet (Aurora), which it said had been operating with a "significant number" of faults.

It said its members planned to take strike action on Saturday 1 August and the following two Saturdays.

An EMR spokesperson said any suggestion that the Hitachi Rail Class 810 fleet did not meet the required safety standards was "incorrect", and added it continued "to engage in discussions with RMT regarding this dispute".

Last week, EMR said reliability and maintenance issues with the new Aurora (Class 810) trains - made by Hitachi Rail - were to blame.

EMR has also outlined "challenges" with both the 810s and the older Class 222s, affecting the toilets, air conditioning and catering equipment.

It added the Class 222 trains had also required "additional maintenance support to accommodate increased running and operational requirements".

The operator first introduced the Aurora trains into passenger service in December, after what EMR said was a three-year delay.

News.title: Family of woman who lay dead in crash for days confronts mechanic who falsified MOT
News.content:
Angry scenes erupted outside court after the family of a woman killed in a car crash confronted a garage owner who falsified an MOT just weeks before.

Neil John Lewis, 47, pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on Tuesday, and admitted he knew the car was "dangerous".

Eve Smith, 21, Darcy Ross, 21, and Rafel Jeanne, 24, died when the car given the false MOT crashed into woodland in Cardiff in March 2023. They lay undiscovered for two days. Two others survived.

As Lewis left court, the family of Ross brandished a framed photograph the dead woman, and shouted at him: "Darcy Ross, remember her name."

News.title: 'Significant hot spots' remain at Cairngorms wildfire
News.content:
Hot spots remain at a wildfire which has burned across 10 square kilometres of land in the Cairngorms over the last week, according to the fire service.

More than 100 firefighters have been involved in the operation to control and extinguish the fire, which started near Ryvoan Bothy, south of Nethy Bridge, last Wednesday.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said on Sunday that they had "surrounded" the large-scale blaze.

However, they say "significant hotspots remain across a large and complex landscape" and crews will stay at the scene until the incident is brought to a safe conclusion.

News.title: Boy, 15, accused of sex attacks on eight girls
News.content:
A 15-year-old boy charged with sexual offences against eight girls, including one who was 10 years old, has appeared in court.

The complainants were aged between 10 and 15 at the time, Wellingborough Youth Court heard.

The teenager, who cannot be named because of his age, faces 22 charges relating to alleged incidents between 2023 and 2025, including rape.

He was not asked to enter any pleas during a 20-minute hearing, before the case was sent to Northampton Crown Court for 18 August.

The defendant, who was accompanied by his mother, was released on bail.

Details of where the offences took place have been withheld to protect the alleged victims' right to anonymity.

The boy has been charged with:

Twelve counts of sexually assaulting a female

Three offences of assaulting a girl under 13 by touching

Two counts of rape and a further two of making an indecent photograph or pseudo-photograph of a child

Assaulting a female by penetration

Possessing a prohibited image of a child and possessing an extreme pornographic image or images

District Judge Amar Mehta told the boy: "Your case is too serious to be tried in this court."

His bail conditions included not to contact the alleged victims and to have no unsupervised contact with females under 16.

The boy spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address. He also asked the judge to explain what the Youth Justice Service was.

News.title: London-based civil servants offered move to No 10 North in Manchester
News.content:
Civil servants working for government departments based in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move to the North of England, the BBC understands.

It comes as the first details are emerging about the new No 10 North, which Downing Street says is already up and running.

The BBC has been told that the Northern branch of Downing Street will be overseen by cabinet minister and ally of Burnham, Louise Haigh.

Haigh, who is the first secretary of state, is thought to have been asked to lead a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC), which will give her control of key decision-making bodies across government.

The OPMC will include No 10, No 10 North and teams within the Cabinet Office.

Addressing his cabinet for the first time, Burnham said No 10 North was "not a gimmick" and that the "time for resisting devolution was over".

A No 10 spokesman said the prime minister was expecting to work from No 10 North "at least one day a week" subject to government business.

Announcing the changes,, external which will also establish a new AI taskforce, Leader of the House of Lords, Baroness Angela Smith said No 10 North would be a "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

It is understood that the initial location of No 10 North will be Heron House in central Manchester, in the same building which houses offices for the intelligence service GCHQ. Specialist police officers have been seen guarding the building.

It is likely that the longer term base for No 10 North will be at a new government "Digital Campus" which is under construction in the Ancoats area of Manchester. It is not due for completion until 2032.

However, a good indication of what it could look like comes from a new report, released on Tuesday.

The blueprint has been authored, external by the Re:State think tank which Burnham was involved with until he stepped down as mayor of Greater Manchester.

News.title: B&M fined £2m over mice infestations
News.content:
B&M Retail Ltd has been fined Â£2m over mice infestations at three Birmingham stores where inspectors found rodent-gnawed foodstuffs and droppings near children's toys.

The company was prosecuted for food hygiene offences by Birmingham City Council after complaints led to inspections being carried out between November 2024 and October 2025.

Locations included St Andrew's Retail Park where officers found gnawed products on sale, the council said. Mouse infestations were also uncovered at Priory Square Shopping Centre and The Fort Shopping Park.

B&M said it was "deeply sorry for the failings identified" and had taken comprehensive action to "strengthen controls across our business".

The council said complaints included one from a member of the public "who reported seeing a mouse in the shop" at Priory Square.

Other transgressions there included urine contamination from rodents on food packaging and shelving, inadequate cleaning standards and structural defects allowing pest entry.

A Hygiene Emergency Prohibition Notice was served and the store was closed immediately, the council said.

A further inspection took place at B&M's store at The Fort Shopping Park in Erdington on 27 October 2025 following a complaint alleging a mouse infestation.

Officers found widespread evidence of mouse activity throughout the premises, including mouse droppings "in close proximity to children's toys on display", the council said.

The store was also closed due to the risks posed to public health.

News.title: Met investigating fatal balcony fall, coroner told
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has opened a corporate manslaughter investigation after a man died following a fall from the balcony of his flat in central London.

Joshua Robbins, 23, leant on the balcony railings of his home in Holland and Thurston Dwellings, Holborn, when it gave way on 26 January. He had been checking on a pizza delivery for him and his father Will Robbins.

The pre-inquest review at St Pancras Coroner's Court heard that Islington and Shoreditch Housing Association (ISHA) was assisting the police with its requests for material.

Joshua's mother, Fiona Garrett, 46, previously said she was seeking answers about her son's death, as his father was "extremely traumatised" after seeing the fall.

A forensic engineer attended the scene and CCTV footage was gathered following the fatal fall.

Det Insp Mark Paterson said: "It's an ongoing investigation. A lot of the material is held by ISHA, who are fully compliant with requests that are being made at this stage."

He said the court could expect an update by January. Senior coroner Mary Hassell scheduled a further pre-inquest review for 6 January 2027.

Previously, Garrett said she had emailed her son's MP, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, requesting a meeting as part of her campaign for answers.

She said she was pleased his office "came back straight away" and began asking for further information.

She said: "I thought, 'Oh well, if I get a reply it would just be your bog-standard, written-by-someone-else response and he just won't even know that it's gone out', but the fact that he wrote it, so he actually signed it himself at the bottom and wrote a little bit extra, it did seem really genuine.

"When I showed Will, he was just like, 'Oh my God, the prime minister knows who our son was'."

A Metropolitan Police spokesperson said inquiries remain ongoing and officers continue to liaise with the Crown Prosecution Service and are keeping the family updated.

News.title: Laos methanol poisoning charges 'slap in face' for families
News.content:
The brother of a British tourist who died in a mass methanol poisoning says the failure to charge anyone over her death is a "slap in the face".

Simone White, 28, was one of six people who died after drinking free shots at the Nana Backpacker Hostel in Vang Vieng, Laos, in November 2024.

Last week authorities in the South-East Asian country said they couldn't determine if the deaths "were caused by the actions of any individual or by any particular cause, because no autopsies were conducted".

Simone's brother, Zak told BBC Newsbeat he found the conclusion "pretty ridiculous", as a death certificate issued in Laos lists "methanol toxicity" as one of her causes of death.

Trainee lawyer Simone and childhood friend Bethany Clarke were among about 100 guests given free shots thought to be tainted with methanol.

They felt unwell the next day and were taken to hospital, where Simone, from Orpington in south-east London, was put on life support before she died.

Two Australians, two Danish citizens and an American also died after drinking the shots.

Medical documents seen by Newsbeat state methanol was found in Bethany's blood in November 2024.

"For them to say there's not really enough evidence, I think for me and my parents, it's a bit of a slap in the face, really," says Zak.

"If you've got a death certificate with that on it, surely there's enough proof?"

Zak previously said his family had braced themselves for an unsatisfying resolution to the case as authorities were "not very forthcoming with trying to speed things along".

The case will remain open for 15 years, but Bethany says she is "not expecting much" from the Laos legal system in future.

"To my mind it's very clear what's happened," she says.

"I don't know why it should take a rocket scientist to come to the conclusion of what's happened here."

The coming 10 days are set to determine whether supermarkets will be hit by food shortages later in the year, farmers say, as parts of England come close to a drought.

Southern and eastern England have had no rain at all this month, the longest spell without rain in 30 years.

England overall has received only 3 per cent of its long-term average July rainfall after the country sweltered in three heatwaves so far.

Land, rivers and streams have dried up, while water use has soared in particularly hot spells.

Prolonged dry weather – the stage immediately before drought – has been declared in East Anglia, the West Midlands, Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly, Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire, Hertfordshire, London, Wessex, Thames, the Solent and the South Downs.

The National Drought Group, whose members include the Met Office, government, regulators, water companies and farmers, says the extreme weather is having a severe effect on the environment and is affecting water supplies and food production.

Farmers say the heat is drying out cereals, while spring barley yields are expected to be hit by a lack of rain earlier in the season.

Some farmers in East Anglia have had to stop abstracting water from rivers because they are so dry.

Harvests have begun early and there is a greater risk of fires breaking out in combine harvesters because of the heat.

England has received only 3 per cent of its long-term average July rain ( PA )

A spokesman for the National Farmers Union (NFU) told The Independent: “Some areas haven’t harvested yet so what happens over the next week to 10 days could have an impact. We’re asking the Environment Agency to be flexible when it comes to abstraction.”

Paul Tompkins, NFU deputy president, said: “Parts of the country, particularly in the east and south, have seen exceptionally low rainfall, creating real challenges for farm businesses. For many arable farmers, this could be another difficult and expensive harvest after extreme weather in both 2024 and 2025 which saw both drought and flood.”

The Met Office is forecasting some rain for the weekend, but it’s most likely in northern parts of the UK.

Thames Water has joined many other water firms that have introduced hosepipe bans, which will take effect from Thursday.

There have been 53 recorded wildfires this year at Sites of Special Scientific Interest, including Dovestone and Tintwistle in the Peak District.

Lower water levels and a lack of rain to top up spawning pools are “significantly” harming breeding of species such as natterjack toads, experts say, while migratory fish, such as Atlantic salmon, cannot move upstream because of lower river flows.

Sea waters around the UK have been hit by marine heatwaves as sea surface temperatures remained well above average.

Oliver Harmar, of Natural England, said: “As well as serious impacts for people, our wonderful wildlife is suffering as the effects of climate change take hold, with the increased likelihood of drought and wildfires.”

He said effects of prolonged dry weather are felt long after the weather cools, reducing populations of wetland birds and amphibians.

Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office, said there are signs of more changeable weather in early August, which may bring rain to some areas.

“However, confidence in the detail remains low, and any rainfall, particularly across southern parts of the UK, is unlikely to be widespread or substantial.

“Many areas are likely to continue experiencing prevailing dry conditions over the coming weeks, especially across southern England.”

French lawmakers on Tuesday adopted a bill banning children under 15 from using social media, making France the first country in the European Union to approve a blanket ban on the platforms as concerns grow worldwide over the harmful effects of digital content on kids.

Both chambers of the Parliament voted in favor of the measure, a flagship initiative of French president Emmanuel Macron’s second term. The bill also bans the use of mobile phones in high schools.

Several families in France have sued TikTok over teen suicides they say are linked to harmful content. Children’s advocates and parents applauded the vote.

“We’ve been campaigning for this bill from the start because, frankly, we have no other option, no other way to counter tech giants,” said Gaëlle Berbonde, a 52-year-old who lives in the Paris region. “The only thing we can do is protect our children, just as we protect our children from drinking alcohol.”

Berbonde told The Associated Press that her daughter was in seventh grade when she got her first smartphone. A parental control app helped monitor what she did online, but Berbonde had no idea what TikTok really was. After a few months, the family realized that the daughter was cutting herself and was suffering from anorexia and depression. She spent a year and a half in hospital but is now 16 and well.

Macron wants the ban in place for the new school year

The legislation is one of the final major measures adopted under Macron’s presidency before he leaves office next year. Macron wants the law to take effect at the start of the new school year in September. However, a review to determine whether the bill complies with the French Constitution is likely to take place and could delay its implementation.

The ban won’t cover online encyclopedias, educational or scientific directories.

Lawmakers from the left-wing party France Unbowed opposed the bill, arguing that its constitutionality is unclear, that it would effectively end online anonymity, and that it would be impossible to enforce.

Ines Legendre, a legal advisor for the online protection group e-Enfance said the law will not immediately translate into an outright ban.

“We’ll also have to address the issue of existing accounts for those under 15. How do we identify them? How do we suspend them? And then there’s the question of age verification for all new accounts that will come into effect,” she said.

According to France’s health watchdog, one in two teenagers spends between two and five hours a day on a smartphone. In a report published in December, it said that some 90% of children between 12 and 17 use smartphones daily to access the internet, with 58% of them using their devices for social networks.

The report highlighted a range of harmful effects stemming from the use of social networks, including reduced self-esteem and increased exposure to content associated with risky behaviors such as self-harm, drug use and suicide.

After the European Commission found that the latest version of the bill overlapped with the EU’s Digital Services Act, which sets strict rules aimed at keeping internet users safe online, lawmakers held final negotiations Monday. They reached an agreement on an amended version of the legislation, which was then submitted to both chambers for a final vote.

___

Catherine Gashka and Alex Turnbull in Paris contributed to this report.

News.title: Father-of-two caught on camera filming women through their windows at night
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A man was caught filming women through their windows at night while dressed in all black before being arrested by police.

Father-of-two Anthony Durkan, 36,of Islington, north London, pleaded guilty to 19 charges of voyeurism at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday.

This follows seven guilty pleas to voyeurism charges on March 26 at the same court – bringing the total number of offences to 26.

Following the guilty pleas, the Metropolitan Police released video footage from his arrest on March 25 earlier this year, and from nearby properties where he attempted to film.

In the footage, Durkan is shown approaching a house on his tip toes with his face covered and peering through windows, before putting his phone past a window railing in order to film inside.

open image in gallery Anthony Durkan filming on a mobile phone through a window of one of his victims ( Met Police/PA )

Body-worn footage then shows a plain clothes officer approaching Durkan as he appeared to be loitering outside a house while holding a mobile phone.

He was told he was under arrest on suspicion of voyeurism.

Durkan replied: “Voyeurism?” before being handcuffed and having his phone seized.

In a police interview, an officer tells Durkan they have identified a “hidden folder” on his phone with galleries containing 162 videos and 99 photos.

An officer then states: “With the exception of maybe three images, all of which just appear to be of landscape or generally pointed at the floor, every single image or video is footage or an image taken of a female who appears to be unaware that she is being filmed.”

Detective Chief Inspector Gemma Alger, whose team led the investigation, said: “Durkan’s offending represented a serious and sustained course of predatory behaviour, deliberately targeting women who were entirely unaware they were being filmed, without their consent and in the privacy of their own homes.

open image in gallery Body-worn footage shows a plain clothes officer approaching Durkan as he appeared to be loitering outside a house while holding a mobile phone ( Metropolitan Police )

“I want to thank the women who had the courage to come forward and report Durkan’s crimes. Their reports, supported by witnesses and swift investigative work, enabled officers to act decisively and arrest Durkan during a proactive patrol.

“This conviction reflects the severity of these crimes and means a dangerous individual has been removed from the streets of London, preventing further harm to women.”

The Metropolitan Police has put out an appeal to women in north London who may have “noticed unusual activity around their home, especially late at night or in the early hours of the morning” between January 2020 and March 2026.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Examination of Durkan’s seized devices uncovered extensive evidence of further voyeurism offences, prompting detectives to review historic crime reports where no suspect had been identified and all viable lines of enquiry exhausted.

“This led to Durkan being linked to offences dating back to January 2020. Detectives are now working to identify additional victims.

“Officers are particularly keen to hear from women in Islington and north London between January 2020 and March 2026 who may have noticed unusual activity around their home, especially late at night or in the early hours of the morning.

“Members of the public are also asked to report suspicious behaviour, such as someone lingering near residential properties, looking through windows, or using a phone or camera.

“Footage captured on doorbell or CCTV cameras could prove vital.”

The investigation team can be contacted directly via e-mail at OpParinga@met.police.uk.

Alternatively, information can be provided anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Durkan was released on conditional bail and will be sentenced at a date to be determined at Snaresbrook Crown Court.

News.content:

How many women hold executive-level positions at top U.S. companies? What is the racial and ethnic breakdown of those roles? What is the gender and racial breakdown of the lowest-paid roles at those companies?

The Trump administration is making it harder for the public to know, moving to toss aside a 60-year-old requirement for tens of thousands of private sector employers to submit workforce demographic reports each year to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the agency responsible for enforcing anti-discrimination laws in the workplace.

The EEOC's Republican majority voted 2-1 Tuesday to rescind the data collection requirement, submitting the proposal to a 30-day public commentary period before final approval. The proposal is a quiet but profound salvo in President Donald Trump's shake up of civil rights enforcement, ending a practice that has endured through 10 Republican and Democratic administrations.

EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, an outspoken critic of diversity and inclusion practices who has urged white men to come forward with discrimination complaints, argued that requiring companies to submit the annual demographic reports risks encouraging companies to justify discriminatory practices to diversify their workforce.

“It may promote racial stereotyping at work, and it may encourage employers to engage in discrimination," Lucas said during a hearing ahead of the vote.

Former Democratic EEOC commissioners and civil rights organizations have denounced the proposal, saying it will deprive the agency of a critical tool for uncovering discrimination patterns and tracking how women and racial minorities have fared since the 1964 Civil Rights Act, which created the EEOC and prohibited employment discrimination based on race, color, sex, national origin and religion.

The EEOC, which receives more than 88,000 worker complaints each year, has historically used the data to guide its enforcement priorities and inform some of its investigations.

Commissioner Kalpana Kotagal, the sole Democrat left on the EEOC since Trump moved to wrest control of the agency, voted against the proposal.

“Today, the commission discusses whether to turn back time to a period before the civil rights movement, kneecapping its ability to protect workers,” Kotagal said.

Here's what to know about the reporting requirement and the proposal to end it:

How the EEOC has collected the data

Since 1966, the EEOC has required companies with at least 100 employees, or federal contractors with at least 50 workers, to submit a form called the EEO-1 each year.

The form, which has evolved over time, identifies 10 job categories from “Executive/Senior Level Officials and Managers” to “Laborers” and “Service Workers.” It asks employers to report on the number male and female workers in each job category, as well as the number of workers from different race and ethnicities.

The data typically covers more than 50 million employees and 73,000 employers nationwide.

A view into gender and race in the private sector

The EEOC launched during the Biden administration an interactive tool allowing the public to explore historical demographic metrics across industries and job categories. The most recent data is from 2023. Under the Trump administration, the EEOC last collected EE0-1 data for the year 2024 but has not publicly disclosed it. Collection of the year 2025 would have begun this year.

The data shows white men dominating executive and senior manager roles at private companies, though women and minorities have made inroads, especially in the years following the #MeToo and Black Lives Matters movements.

Women remain underrepresented in the top ranks of companies. While they make up nearly half the workforce at the companies surveyed, women held just 34.5% of executives and senior manager roles in 2023. That was up from 29.2% a decade earlier.

White and Asian women made the fastest gains, and by 2023, were no longer underrepresented in senior roles compared to their numbers in the overall workforce. In contrast, Black and Hispanic women remained sharply underrepresented in executive and senior manager roles despite making modest gains.

Asian men have been proportionally represented in senior roles for years, while Black and Hispanic men remained underrepresented in 2023.

Of those demographic groups, only one was overrepresented in senior roles: white men, who made up a third of the overall workforce at the companies surveyed but held 52.7% of executive and senior management roles.

Why the government wants to end the data collection

Lucas said the annual reporting requirements impose “hundreds of millions of dollars” on costs on employers, a burden she argued was unnecessary absent “any allegation, indication, or evidence of discrimination.”

The move was recommended by Project 2025, the conservative Heritage Foundation’s blueprint that has guided many of the Trump administration’s policies.

A group of former Democratic EEOC commissioners and legal counselors said there is little evidence that companies are routinely using employment data to engage in quotas or race-based hiring.

“This is simply inaccurate and unsupported speculation, at odds with the ways in which this data is actually collected, managed and used,” the former officials said in a statement.

Instead, the officials said, tracking such data encourages companies to proactively examine their hiring, promotion, benefits and other policies to ensure they are not unnecessarily erecting barriers. The agency has also issued special reports on demographic employment trends across certain industries or roles.

Corporate retreat from demographic disclosure

The EEOC is prohibited from publicly releasing an individual company’s EEO-1 form, only publishing the information in the aggregate. In recent years, however, a growing number of the country’s top companies began publicly releasing their forms in response to pressure from shareholders and Democratic elected officials to show transparency in their diversity efforts.

That trend has started to reverse.

Companies have started to pull back on publicizing both EEO-1 forms and their own diversity reports, which conservative advocates and the Trump administration have seized on to argue that companies are using discriminatory tactics to add women and minorities to their ranks.

In 2025, 24 companies in the S&P 100 — the largest U.S. publicly traded companies — chose not to disclose their EEO-1 data after having done so the year before, according to Andrew Jones, principal researcher at The Conference Board Governance & Sustainability Center. Still, 60 S&P 100 companies did release the data.

Why companies may keep gathering data

Companies are still likely to keep track of their demographic data, whether or not they disclose any of those metrics publicly, and even if they are no longer required to submit annual EEO-1 reports. That's because Title VII requires employers to keep records that could be pertinent to any discrimination investigation, and the EEOC is empowered to request them.

“What we are generally advising is to stay the course,” Jennifer Robins, counsel in law firm Saul Ewing’s Labor and Employment Group. “Private litigants, employment discrimination lawsuits are not going away, and this data is helpful to defending oneself.”

The EEOC has demanded extensive demographic data from companies to bolster Lucas' own marquee cases. Those include an investigation into diversity, equity and inclusion practices of sports giant Nike, which Lucas has alleged discriminate against white employees.

Lucas emphasized Tuesday that the EEOC would continue to demand data in the course of its investigations. Kotagal warned employers that under future leadership, the EEOC could reinstitute the EEO-1 collection.

News.title: Donald Trump furious at Miliband’s appointment as foreign secretary
News.content:

The White House is “deeply concerned” about Ed Miliband’s appointment as foreign secretary, with a warning that Donald Trump has not forgotten scathing remarks the former Labour leader has made about him in the past.

New prime minister Andy Burnham has been cautioned that Mr Miliband has some “serious diplomatic repair to undertake” in the US, after his promotion to the role on Monday sparked anger from the Trump administration.

The former energy secretary has previously clashed with Mr Trumpover net zero and his attitudes to democracy and in 2016 he described the president as “a racist, misogynistic, self-confessed groper”.

One source close to the president told The Independent: “There’s genuine anger about this appointment.”

open image in gallery Ed Miliband’s appointment has ruffled feathers in Washington DC ( PA )

The two men have been attacking one another for more than a decade. Mr Miliband previously said of the president: “We must do our best at home and abroad to resist the worst of Trumpism… These are dark days for America and the world. There can be little solace right now.”

In 2017, he said Mr Trump had “lowered the bar for idiocy” and later joined a Stop Trump March in London. He also criticised the president’s "incredibly peculiar relationship with Russia" and accused him of lowering standards in politics.

The new foreign secretary has also described Mr Trump’s criticism on social media of the UK’s stance on drilling for oil and gas as “irrelevant”, with the president highly critical of his “net zero zealotry" and accusing him of blocking the UK from expanding oil and gas operations in the North Sea.

On Mr Miliband’s past remarks, one ally close to the president told The Independent: “Trump doesn’t forget. He will not forget. Miliband has some serious diplomatic repair to undertake.”

A consultant who works with both the White House and State Department added: “It [Mr Miliband’s appointment] is going down like a lead balloon. The US government no longer takes the UK seriously.

“Ed Miliband is known in Washington for all the wrong reasons. Ed Miliband is seen as an unreasonable ‘nut zero’ extremist who blocked North Sea oil production but was happy for the UK to purchase Norway's fossil fuels from the North Sea.”

The White House is said to be “deeply concerned” about the appointment even though Mr Miliband has previously described how much he loves the US.

open image in gallery Trump is not happy with Miliband’s past remarks about him ( Getty )

They also noted that Mr Burnham himself said in 2021: “Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed.”

Mr Burnham chose Mr Miliband as foreign secretary partly because he decided against making him chancellor, following a backlash from those on the right of the party.

However, the plan, as revealed over the weekend by The Independent, is for Mr Miliband to reform the Foreign Office around the UK’s climate goals and find a roadmap back to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on overseas aid, which was slashed under Sir Keir Starmer.

But there is also anger in the US over Mr Miliband’s time as Labour leader when he withdrew his support for bombing Syria after the regime there was responsible for a number of atrocities in 2013. The coalition government lost the vote in parliament as a result and the US was left alone in wanting to take action.

Former prime minister Boris Johnson, who is close to senior Republicans, suggested on Tuesday that this emboldened Vladimir Putin to invade the Crimea in Ukraine in 2014.

He wrote on X: “The failure to stand up to Bashar al-Assad – for which Miliband bears much guilt – led directly to Putin’s first invasion of Ukraine. An appalling choice for foreign secretary. The Kremlin will be delighted.”

Mr Miliband lived in Boston, Massachusetts, as a boy for brief periods while his father, the Marxist academic Ralph Miliband, was teaching there. He is big fan of baseball and a supporter of the Boston Red Sox. He later returned to the US as an adult in the early 2000s to spend several semesters teaching economics at Harvard University.

open image in gallery Burnham hosts his first cabinet meeting on Tuesday ( PA )

Another ally of the president working on his Iranian policy told The Independent that Mr Miliband was not the only choice raising eyebrows in the US.

They said: “Miliband is a bit of an odd choice – as is Wes Streeting as defence secretary.”

But former Labour foreign minister Bill Rammell said he believes Mr Miliband and Mr Trump will be able to put their differences behind them.

He pointed out that both Sir Keir and the former foreign secretary David Lammy had developed a good relationship with President Trump despite their previous remarks about him.

Added to that, JD Vance had never been a Trump supporter before becoming his pick for vice-president in 2024.

Mr Rammell told GB News: “I am sure Ed Miliband will be able to build a working relationship.”

In a statement following his appointment, Mr Miliband appeared to look towards the EU first, promising to deepen ties with the bloc before speaking about Britain’s “essential alliance with the United States”.

Mr Miliband pledged to fight for “Britain’s interests and our values of democracy, freedom and the rule of law on the world stage”.

He added: “I will seek to deepen and strengthen our strategic alliance with the European Union, which is so important for our prosperity and security and at the same time nurture our strong, enduring and essential alliance with the United States.”

Steve Bannon, an outspoken ally of President Trump, told The Telegraph: “The Trump administration took the extraordinary step of warning the new prime minister that the United States would view the appointment of “red diaper” baby and self-described socialist Ed Miliband as very injurious to the ‘special relationship’. Burnham could not care less – he appointed this twit anyway.”

The Independent has contacted Mr Miliband’s office but they have declined to comment.

Charlize Theron is coming clean about ogling Matt Damon’s ripped physique after he transformed to film The Odyssey.

Damon, 55, lost more than 20 pounds and underwent intense training to get in shape to play Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s Greek epic.

When an interviewer with Entertainment Tonight pointed out Damon’s muscles at the movie’s world premiere in London, Theron — who plays Greek goddess Calypso in the film — admitted that she was checking him out as well.

“I've seen him without all of that suit on. He's incredible. Incredible,” the Oscar-winning actor, 50, gushed to ET. “It’s weird. I’m, like, staring at him weirdly. I’m looking at his ass.”

She then joked, “I shouldn’t do that! That’s just wrong,” before doubling down on how “amazing” he looked.

open image in gallery Charlize Theron and Matt Damon co-star in Christopher Nolan's new film 'The Odyssey' ( Getty )

The two A-list actors go way back. They co-starred in The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will Smith in 2000 and have remained friends over the years.

Theron said on the Today show earlier this month that reuniting with Damon on set was “sentimental.”

“We did the first take, and I just went, ‘Oh my God, we did this when we were babies, and here we are, two old humans,’” she said on the show July 13, adding that Damon is “just one of my favorite people.”

She added: “It’s rare that you get to do something like that, you know, to experience the same experience, like 30 years later, and with someone as great and as wonderful.”

open image in gallery Matt Damon stars as Odysseus in ‘The Odyssey’ ( Universal Pictures )

In addition to Theron and Damon, Nolan’s adaptation starred Tom Holland as Telemachus, Robert Pattinson as Antinous and Zendaya as Athena. It also features Anne Hathaway, Elliot Page and Lupita Nyong’o.

For his lead role, Damon has previously opened up about the physical training that he underwent to take on the role after Nolan asked him to be “lean but strong.”

“I was in great shape. I lost a lot of weight,” the Good Will Hunting actor told Jason and Travis Kelce on their New Heights podcast in January.

Damon, who has been married to Luciana Barroso since 2005, said he weighed between 185 and 200 pounds before filming the movie, but worked with his doctor to cut gluten from his diet — which proved to be the key to his transformation.

“I did that whole movie at 167,” he said. “And I haven’t been that light since high school. So it was a lot of training and a really strict diet.”
