World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. Last week, Latvian interior minister Jānis Dombrava told Euronews that his country has now “become the main target” for Belarus’s migrant trafficking, instead of Poland and Lithuania. On Thursday, Latvia recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, compared to two in Lithuania on the same day and zero in Poland the previous day. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland up 30% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. Ukraine’s foreign minister has called on "Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians” after an incident in which a man was filmed shouting xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian girls on a bus in Poland. The perpetrator has been detained https://t.co/AfGCNqtJbj — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Figures from Poland’s government, which is a coalition ranging from left to centre right, have also condemned recent incidents of hate towards Ukrainians. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called last week’s incident in a bus “disgusting” and warned of the potential “disastrous consequences” of inciting national hatred. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński promised that the state would deal with “any form of aggression”, but also blamed the right-wing opposition for stirring antipathy. However, PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek accused the government of “cynically exploiting” the incident in Bielsko-Biała “for political purposes”. He said it was, in fact, Tusk and Kierwiński who were “responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, hailed the fact that “the entire political class” in Poland had condemned the incident on the bus and expressed hope that the recent wave of attacks is a “temporary symptom” that “will pass”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Two Polish far-right activists have been charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business providing services to immigrants. World.title: President vetoes legal rights for same-sex couples in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to sign an agreement granting them certain rights. The proposed law would have marked the first time that Poland had recognised same-sex relationships in domestic law. However, Nawrocki argued that such a move would threaten the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. The measures in question were approved by both houses of parliament in May and June with the support of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The proposed law would have allowed couples, both same-sex and opposite-sex, to enter into a new type of contract, signed before a notary and then submitted to the registry office. It would have granted them some of the rights available to married couples, including joint property and tax settlement, access to their partner’s medical information, exemption from inheritance and gift taxes, and the right to decide about their partner’s burial if they died. However, the two main opposition parties – the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) – voted against the legislation, and Nawrocki himself also made clear that he intended to veto it. The government’s majority in parliament has approved a bill that would grant same-sex partners some of the rights available to married couples. However, President Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has made clear he will veto the law https://t.co/hx8viUN6QH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 29, 2026 On Friday morning, the president confirmed he would not be signing into law the two bills passed by parliament that would have introduced the new system. He said that the measures would effectively “introduce civil partnerships through the back door”, and that such partnerships are “intended to replace or substitute the institution of marriage”. “As the guardian of the constitution, I cannot accept a solution that would lead to the loss of the special status of marriage defined in article 18 of the constitution as a union between a woman and a man, placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” he added. Nawrocki also argued that the proposed measures were contrary to the principles of social justice because they would have granted such couples some of the privileges of marriage but without all of the same obligations. He also noted that the proposed new type of contract could be terminated far more easily than a marriage. “Marriage, which best secures family stability, cannot become one of many equally valid options offered by the state administration,” declared the president. “The family is a community fundamental to the survival of the nation.” However, Nawrocki added that, as he has previously said, he remains open to legislation that would grant loved ones rights relating to healthcare and various administrative issues. But only if it “does not create an alternative to marriage” or “introduce ideological changes to family law”. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision was condemned by Tusk, who called it “an expression of contempt toward people and their right to happiness and a normal life”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, accused the president of “turning his back on the two million Poles living today in informal relationships”. However, she pledged that “the veto will not halt social change”. If such change “cannot go through the door, then [it will go] through the window”. Kotula noted that Poland has already begun legally recognising same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union member states, after being ordered to do so by the European Court of Justice. While “not all benefits are yet available” to such couples, “this is something that I intend to deliver”, she added. Prezydenckie weto to wyraz pogardy wobec ludzi i ich prawa do szczęścia i normalnego życia. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 However, the government’s ability and willingness to take such action, even when it cannot be vetoed by Nawrocki, is hampered by internal disagreements over the issue within Tusk’s coalition. The Left (Lewica), from which Kotula hails, and Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party are generally in favour of strengthening LGBT+ rights. But they have met with resistance from more conservative elements in the coalition, in particular the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). The measures vetoed today by Nawrocki were already a compromise within the government: earlier plans to introduce same-sex civil partnerships were watered down to instead simply allow same-sex couples to sign a contract granting them certain rights. However, opinion polls show that the Polish public itself is in mostly in favour of recognising same-sex relationships. State research agency CBOS last year found its highest-ever level of support for the introduction of civil partnerships, with 62% of Poles in favour. Polish prosecutors have indicted an 18-year-old Ukrainian accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tensions between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of slogans in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which massacred Poles during World War Two. Among the sites where he placed graffiti were a monument to Polish victims of those massacres (pictured above), as well as a memorial dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. If found guilty, the suspect could face up to life in prison. The history of the UPA has been at the heart of an ongoing diplomatic dispute between Warsaw and Kyiv. However, the actions in this particular case took place in 2024 and 2025, before the current crisis emerged. Prokurator z dolnośląskiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego we Wrocławiu akt oskarżenia przeciwko Illii K., któremu zarzucono popełnienie 47 przestępstw związanych z działalnością dywersyjną i sabotażową na rzecz obcego wywiadu. 45 zarzutów dotyczy umieszczania na… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 16, 2026 The suspect in the case was detained in August 2025, shortly after graffiti glorifying the UPA had appeared on a monument in Poland honouring victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles. On Thursday, prosecutors announced that they have issued an indictment against the suspect, whom they named only as Illia K. under Polish privacy law. He is accused of 47 crimes in total. Of those, 45 are for “acts of subversion and sabotage for the benefit of foreign intelligence, consisting primarily of writing slogans in Ukrainian on the facades of buildings and in memorial sites with the text ‘Glory to the UPA’ and red-and-black flags attributed to the UPA “, prosecutors said. Those actions “were aimed at inciting hatred on national grounds, deepening antagonisms between Poles and Ukrainians, causing social unrest and creating a sense of helplessness of state authorities”. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. The issue has recently flared up again after President Volodymyr Zelensky in late May named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour. Russia has also long sought to exploit such tensions, and Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) notes that Illia K.’s actions were carried out “at the request of the Russian security services”, which were seeking to “incite conflicts between the Polish and Ukrainian nations”. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 In addition, Illia K. also faces one charge of participation in an organised criminal group and another of preparing for an act of subversion or sabotage that would have involved flying a drone over Poland’s Armed Forces Day parade in Warsaw last year, which was attended by President Nawrocki. Prosecutors note that the accused “acted for financial, not ideological, reasons”. He was paid for his actions in cryptocurrencies. That is typical of the so-called “disposable agents” Russia increasingly uses, who are amateurs – often young Ukrainians or Belarusians – hired and paid through messaging service Telegram. The suspect has been held in pretrial detention since he was arrested by the ABW last year. If found guilty, he could face up to life in prison. Prosecutors say that, although Illia K. initially admitted to the charges against him, he later decided to change his stance and has pleaded not guilty while exercising his right to remain silent. The head of Poland's security services has appealed to Ukrainians, the country's largest immigrant group, not to be tempted to earn money by acting as Russian agents. Russia regularly recruits Ukrainians in Poland to carry out espionage and sabotage https://t.co/aa5UUWWBrx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2025 Poland has in recent years detained, charged and in some cases convicted dozens of agents accused of carrying out espionage, sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” on behalf of Russia and its ally Belarus. In March, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism (ICCT) reported that Poland is now the “primary focus of Russian activity” when it comes to sabotage. In June, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski warned that Moscow is “waging a full-scale cognitive war against us” and that there is a “Russian fifth column” operating in Poland. World.title: Prague Airport Unions Declare Strike Readiness Over New CEO Appointment
World.content:
Five trade unions at Václav Havel Prague Airport and ČSA Handling have announced strike readiness over the appointment of Radomír Lašák as the new head of Letiště Praha.

The unions’ announcement does not currently affect airport operations. Prague Airport confirmed that all flights are operating normally and passengers should not expect disruptions, delays, or cancellations.

The labour groups oppose Lašák’s appointment, pointing to his previous role in the management of Czech Airlines before the carrier entered bankruptcy proceedings. They have also raised concerns about the transparency of the selection process for the airport’s top executive position.

Trade union representatives are seeking more information about possible future changes to the airport’s management structure, financial strategy, and personnel policy. They argue that employees have not received sufficient guarantees about the company’s future direction.

Additional concerns emerged after Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the government was considering a possible stock market listing of part of Prague Airport’s shares. Unions fear that such a move could bring changes to the airport’s operations and affect job security.

Finance Minister Alena Šillerová rejected the concerns, saying there was no reason for employees to worry. According to her, Lašák was selected as the strongest candidate through an open recruitment process, and the government is not planning mass layoffs or major organisational changes.

Šillerová is scheduled to meet with trade union representatives on Tuesday to discuss their concerns directly.

The announced strike readiness remains in effect from July 21 until it is officially withdrawn. If Lašák’s appointment receives final approval from the government’s personnel committee, he will replace Jiří Pos, whose term as head of Prague Airport ends at the end of August.

World.title: Prague Petřín Cable Car Ticket Price to Rise to 100 CZK After Reopening
World.content:
Passengers using the iconic Petřín Cable Car will pay more when the service resumes in September.

The city council has approved a new fare of 100 CZK for a single ride, up from the previous 60 CZK.

The increase comes after a two-year shutdown during which the historic line underwent major reconstruction. The cable car has been out of operation since September 2024, with new vehicles built in Switzerland now undergoing final testing before returning to service.

The first passengers are expected to board the renewed cable car in September, but the experience will come at a higher cost.

Passengers who purchase tickets electronically will pay a discounted fare of 90 CZK.

Children under 15 and seniors over 65 will continue to travel free of charge. The ride will also remain included in Prague’s 24-hour and 72-hour public transport tickets, as well as long-term travel passes.

The Petřín Cable Car, one of Prague’s most popular attractions, connects the Újezd area with Petřín Hill and provides access to one of the city’s most visited viewpoints. The service has been closed while the track, technology and vehicles were being upgraded.

The newly manufactured cars feature a modern design and are currently completing mandatory operational tests before the official reopening.

World.title: Five Legendary Ballets in One Night at Prague’s Hybernia Theatre
World.content:
Prague’s Hybernia Theatre is hosting a series of special evenings dedicated to classical ballet, bringing together some of the most celebrated scenes from the world’s best-known productions.

The upcoming Classic Ballet Gala will take place on July 22, 25 and 29.

More info about the program here.

The performance will feature students and graduates of the conservatory, presenting excerpts from legendary ballets including Don Quixote, Swan Lake, The Nutcracker, Sleeping Beauty and Le Corsaire.

Rather than focusing on a single full-length production, the gala will offer audiences the opportunity to experience highlights from several major works in one evening.

The young dancers will perform in specially prepared costumes and under the guidance of experienced teachers, including former soloists of the National Theatre Ballet. The artistic concept and dramaturgy of the evening are overseen by Pamela Morávková and Jiří Horák.

The programme will combine the dramatic energy of Don Quixote, the romantic atmosphere of Swan Lake, the fantasy world of The Nutcracker, the fairy-tale elegance of Sleeping Beauty, and the adventure of Le Corsaire.

Founded in 1945, the Prague Dance Conservatory is the oldest and largest institution of its kind in the Czech Republic. Over eight decades, the school has educated generations of dancers, choreographers, ballet masters and teachers who have performed on stages in the Czech Republic and abroad.

Its students regularly take part in international competitions and represent Czech dance at festivals and cultural events around the world.

World.title: Look Up! JAS 39 Gripen Jets to Fly Over Prague on Wednesday
World.content:
Prague residents will have the chance to see JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets flying above the city on Wednesday, July 22.

The aircraft will take part in a ceremonial event at the National Memorial on Vítkov.

The flyover is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. and will be carried out as a training flight connected with the ceremony.

According to information from Prague 4 City Hall, the jets will approach the capital from the east, flying over areas including Běchovice, Dolní Počernice and Žižkov.

The aircraft will then turn south over Prague Castle before continuing their return route through Podolí, Nusle and Hostivař. After completing the flight over the city, the jets will head back to their base in Pardubice.

The route means residents in several parts of Prague may be able to see the aircraft, depending on weather conditions and visibility.

Military aircraft flights over the capital are relatively rare but not unusual. In March 2024, crowds gathered in central Prague to watch a large military flyover marking the 25th anniversary of the Czech Republic joining NATO.

That event included five fighter jets and an Airbus aircraft, which flew over landmarks including Charles Bridge. The fighter jets later returned to their bases, while the Airbus landed at Prague’s Václav Havel Airport.

The Czech Air Force regularly uses ceremonial flights to mark important national events and military anniversaries, while also serving as training exercises for pilots.

World.title: Twelve Prague Tram Lines Changed Due to Repairs in City Center
World.content:
Tram services on Spálená Street and Národní třída in central Prague have been suspended due to track repairs.

The closure, which began on Saturday, will continue until August 10 and affects 12 tram lines operating through the city center.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has not introduced replacement bus services during the disruption. Passengers are advised to use the metro as an alternative, especially for journeys through the busiest parts of the city.

The affected section runs between the Újezd and Lazarská stops and impacts tram lines 2, 4, 5, 9, 18, 22, 23, 42, 93, 97, 98 and 99.

Several routes have been temporarily modified. Some trams are being redirected through the National Theatre stop on Masarykovo nábřeží, while others are operating via Myslíkova Street and Jiráskovo náměstí, or through Anděl and Švandovo divadlo. Some lines have received more significant route changes.

Two Temporary Tram Lines Added During Repairs

To help manage the disruption, DPP has introduced two temporary tram services.

Line 32 connects Vypich with Sídliště Řepy, while line 39 runs between Vozovna Žižkov and Náměstí Bratří Synků.

A new temporary stop has also been created at Malostranská. During daytime operations, trams will stop on the Edvarda Beneše embankment in the direction of Čechův most. During night service, the stop will operate on Letenská Street in both directions.

Track Repairs Include New Switches and Overhead Line Upgrades

The ongoing construction focuses on replacing worn sections of the tram infrastructure at the intersection of Spálená and Lazarská streets.

Workers will also repair track curves, install two new grease traps near the Máj department store, modernize two tram switches and replace aging overhead line poles near the National Theatre.

Additional local repairs to the tram network will also be carried out during the closure period.

World.title: Why Film Fans Traveled Hundreds of Kilometers to See “The Odyssey” in Prague
World.content:
Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey attracted film fans from across Europe to Prague, where Cinema City Flora hosted a sold-out 70mm IMAX premiere.

Tickets for the opening night sold out within hours of going on sale, with visitors traveling from several countries to experience the film as Nolan intended.

The adaptation of Homer’s ancient epic has been among the year’s most anticipated releases since its announcement. While its cast and source material generated significant attention, much of the excitement centered on its technical achievement.

The Odyssey is the first feature film shot entirely on 70mm IMAX film, making screenings in compatible theaters exceptionally rare.

Cinema City Flora is among roughly four dozen cinemas worldwide equipped to project 70mm IMAX film. Until earlier this month, it was the only venue in continental Europe with that capability.

Following the opening of new theaters in France and Belgium, it is now one of just three across mainland Europe still offering the format. It also remains the continent’s longest-operating 70mm IMAX venue.

Because 70mm IMAX projectors are no longer manufactured and require specialized maintenance, very few cinemas can continue operating the technology.

That scarcity has turned Prague into a destination for moviegoers willing to travel hundreds, and in some cases thousands, of kilometers to see major releases in their original presentation.

Set after the conclusion of the 10-year Trojan War, the story follows the hero Odysseus (Matt Damon) as he returns to Ithaca, a journey that takes nearly as much time as the war.

Borrowing from the Greek tradition of oral storytelling, Nolan’s nearly three-hour adaptation is told through the accounts of a bard (played by Travis Scott) who spins tales of the great warrior and Odysseus himself as he reflects on the events of his homecoming voyage.

World.title: Two Dead After Axe and Knife Attack at Prague Hostel
World.content:
Two people died and another person was seriously injured after a violent axe and knife attack at a hostel in Prague.

Police officers responding to the scene shot and killed the attacker, who had also threatened them.

The incident happened on Thursday evening at a hostel on Vídeňská Street in Prague 4, according to Czech news outlet Novinky.cz, which first reported on the case.

The hostel is located near the Institute of Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM), and the attacker and victims were reportedly employees of the medical facility.

Police said the suspect attacked people inside the building before turning on responding officers. The officers used their weapons against him, and the attacker was killed at the scene. Authorities later confirmed that no further threat to the public remained.

Emergency crews treated four people following the incident. Two victims suffered cardiac arrest and rescuers immediately began resuscitation efforts. Despite their attempts, both patients died.

A third person suffered serious injuries caused by a sharp weapon. After receiving medical treatment, the injured person was transported to a trauma centre while conscious.

The fourth person involved in the incident was not physically injured but required medical attention due to psychological and internal complications, according to emergency responders.

Police continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding the attack, including the motive of the suspect.

World.title: A Night with Mozart: Candlelit Concert and Fine Dining in Historic Ballroom
World.content:
Few cities are as closely connected to Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart as Prague.

More than two centuries after Don Giovanni premiered here, visitors can still experience his music in a setting that captures the atmosphere of the era.

The Mozart Dinner at the Grand Hotel Bohemia combines a live opera performance with a three-course dinner in the hotel’s spectacular Boccaccio Hall, one of Prague’s finest historic ballrooms.

The concert features leading opera singers accompanied by a string quintet, performing some of Mozart’s best-known arias and duets from The Marriage of Figaro, The Magic Flute, and Don Giovanni.

The latter holds a special place in Prague’s history, having premiered at the city’s Estates Theatre in 1787.

The performance is designed to be more intimate than a traditional opera concert. Instead of remaining on stage throughout the evening, the singers move through the hall, performing among the audience and making guests feel part of the experience.

The evening is divided into three musical performances, with each followed by a course of dinner. Rather than separating the concert from the meal, the format allows the two to complement one another, creating a relaxed pace that encourages guests to enjoy both.

The menu draws on traditional Czech and Austrian cuisine, reflecting the region’s culinary heritage while matching the historic surroundings.

Each course has been carefully selected to accompany the evening without distracting from the music.

World.title: Fidesz’s parliamentary group elected new leader after previous one stepping down
World.content:
Hungary’s ruling Fidesz party has elected János Bóka as the new leader of its parliamentary group, replacing Gergely Gulyás, who stepped down earlier this month.

The decision was made unanimously at the party’s parliamentary group meeting on Tuesday following a proposal by former prime minister and Fidesz chairman Viktor Orbán, who had consulted the party’s national leadership before putting Bóka’s name forward. Orbán later confirmed the appointment in a Facebook post, while Bóka also announced his new role on social media.

Succeeding Gergely Gulyás

Fidesz was forced to appoint a new parliamentary group leader after Gergely Gulyás announced on 13 July that he would resign from the post. He said his departure was linked to amendments to Hungary’s Fundamental Law, under which he would no longer be eligible to serve as an MP in the next parliamentary term.

Until his appointment, Bóka had served as one of the parliamentary group’s deputy leaders, making him one of the most frequently mentioned candidates to succeed Gulyás. Hungarian media had reported for weeks that Orbán favoured him for the position.

Although Fidesz MP János Pócs suggested shortly before Tuesday’s meeting that the outcome had not yet been decided, Bóka’s appointment had been widely expected.

Political attacks before the announcement

The prospect of Bóka taking over the parliamentary group leadership had already become a point of political debate. Prime Minister Péter Magyar repeatedly criticised the incoming leader in Parliament, referring to him on Tuesday as the “future parliamentary group leader” even before the official announcement.

During his speech, PM Magyar described Bóka as a “former SZDSZ politician turned Fidesz crisis manager” and accused him of contributing to Hungary’s failure to secure European Union funding. Magyar also contrasted Bóka with his predecessor, saying that compared with Bóka’s “meaningless speech”, Gulyás “was a hurricane on his own”.

From academia to government

Bóka graduated in law from the University of Szeged in 2001 and obtained his PhD there in 2013. His early career included a period at Hungary’s Information Office between 2003 and 2004. He later worked as an assistant to former SZDSZ Member of the European Parliament István Szent-Iványi until 2009, and that same year stood as an SZDSZ candidate in the European Parliament elections.

Alongside his political career, Bóka held several academic positions, serving as an assistant lecturer, lecturer, associate professor and vice dean, while also working as a senior adviser at the Civil Division of Hungary’s Curia, the country’s supreme court.

He entered government in 2018 as a state secretary at the Ministry of Justice before moving to the Prime Minister’s Office in 2021. In 2022 he became ministerial commissioner, and from 2023 until 2026 served as Hungary’s minister responsible for European Union affairs.

During his time overseeing EU affairs, Bóka faced criticism from opponents over Hungary’s access to frozen EU funds. Following this year’s party leadership reshuffle, he also became one of Fidesz’s vice-presidents.

Stay up-to-date: “Unprecedented action”, says Orbán’s head of press while claiming prosecution investigates Fidesz’s communication system

A key role ahead of the next election

As parliamentary group leader, Bóka will be responsible for coordinating Fidesz’s legislative agenda and managing the ruling party’s MPs in the National Assembly. The appointment places him in one of the party’s most influential parliamentary positions as Hungary moves towards the next general election.

World.title: “Unprecedented action”: Orbán’s head of press claims prosecution investigates Fidesz’s communication system
World.content:
According to a statement issued by Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz’s communications director and former press chief to ex-prime minister Viktor Orbán, investigators from the prosecution service arrived without prior notice on Tuesday at a facility hosting the party’s servers.

Investigators arrived uninvited

Havasi claimed the investigators intended to seize Fidesz’s entire communications system and databases. He described the development as unprecedented in Hungary since 1990, stating that “authoritarianism has reached a new level today”. According to Havasi, the Tisza Party had failed to defeat Fidesz through political means and was now attempting to “legally cripple” the governing party.

He added that Fidesz would not yield to either political or legal pressure and would continue to resist what he characterised as the Tisza Party’s “authoritarian” methods.

Prosecutors link operation to NKA investigation

Shortly after Havasi’s statement, the Central Investigation Prosecutor’s Office denied that its investigators were carrying out the reported procedural actions. It later emerged that the operation was instead conducted by the Bács-Kiskun County Chief Prosecutor’s Office as part of its investigation into the National Cultural Fund (NKA).

Dr. Marianna Bodó, spokesperson for the county prosecutor’s office, confirmed that an investigation is ongoing on suspicion of breach of fiduciary duty and other alleged criminal offences connected to the NKA case. She stated that the procedural measures referred to by Fidesz were carried out as part of that investigation but declined to provide further details, citing the interests of the ongoing proceedings.

The NKA investigation is linked to the wider scandal surrounding approximately HUF 17 billion (around EUR 47 million) in cultural grants allegedly distributed within Fidesz circles before the elections. The case previously led to the arrest of several individuals, including former Óbuda mayor Balázs Bús, who also served as vice-president of the National Cultural Fund.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar calls for clarification

Prime Minister Péter Magyar also reacted to Fidesz’s announcement in a Facebook post. “The Fidesz party itself has announced that investigators carried out a search and seizure today in connection with Viktor Orbán’s party’s servers. We are waiting for the prosecution service’s briefing,” he wrote.

In a follow-up comment, Magyar said the government was awaiting clarification on what case was being investigated and what, if anything, had been seized during the operation.

Stay up-to-date: Hungary’s former government quietly invested almost EUR 300 million in Rheinmetall’s tank development

Political tensions intensify

The incident is likely to further heighten political tensions between the governing Fidesz party and Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party.

While Fidesz portrays the investigative action as politically motivated and an attempt to weaken the party through legal means, prosecutors have maintained that the measures form part of the broader NKA corruption investigation and have not disclosed additional details about the operation. At this stage, it remains unclear whether any data or equipment belonging to Fidesz was ultimately seized.

World.title: Property market weakens in Hungary, but above average market still holds on
World.content:
Demand in Hungary’s residential property market has remained subdued this year, with overall transaction volumes declining. However, the market for above-average-priced homes has followed a different trajectory.

Transactions of properties above HUF 100 million increase despite weaker overall market

According to an analysis by Duna House, the total number of property transactions fell by around 7% compared with the same period last year, while sales of properties worth more than HUF 100 million (appr. EUR 276,000) rose by 18%.

Their share of all transactions increased from 8% to more than 10%. This growth, however, has not been driven by the premium segment: transaction volumes for genuine premium properties worth more than HUF 300 million (around EUR 828,000) have remained unchanged, while activity in the highest price bracket has declined.

Inflation has redefined what counts as an expensive property

Rising property prices have also reshaped what is considered expensive. The median selling price of properties sold by Duna House reached around HUF 50 million (EUR 138,000) in the first half of this year, up from HUF 42 million (EUR 116,000) a year earlier.

Against this backdrop, the HUF 100 million threshold no longer represents the premium market, but rather roughly the top 10% of the market by value – a segment best described as above-average-priced properties. It only becomes meaningful to speak of the premium segment above HUF 300 million, where the market operates according to a distinct set of dynamics.

Strong upper-middle-class demand and rising prices drive growth

The expansion in sales of above-average-priced properties is driven by two factors. Firstly, there is genuine demand, as upper-middle-class buyers remain active in the housing market. Secondly, there is a technical effect: as property prices have risen across the board, an increasing number of transactions now exceed the HUF 100 million threshold.

By contrast, the genuine premium segment – properties valued above HUF 300 million – has not expanded over the past six months. “The market for above-average-priced, but not yet premium, properties is performing differently because it is driven by a different type of demand than the broader market,” said Péter Szegő, Chief Analyst at Duna House.

“The Otthon Start scheme has stimulated demand below its eligibility limits – HUF 100 million for flats and HUF 150 million (EUR 414,000) for detached houses – and in doing so has pushed the overall price level higher. Rather than diverting demand away from more expensive properties, the subsidised mortgage has boosted activity below the threshold, indirectly lifting more transactions above the HUF 100 million mark. The premium segment, on the other hand, is driven not by subsidised lending but by financially strong buyers, who are typically moving into larger, higher-value homes.”

Financing differs in the higher-end market

Financing in the above-average-priced segment also differs from that of the wider market. Since flats priced above HUF 100 million and single-family homes above HUF 150 million are not eligible for the Otthon Start scheme, buyers in this segment generally finance purchases with their own capital, often supplemented by market-rate mortgage loans.

“In this segment, mortgage financing often plays a supporting role rather than acting as the primary driver of a transaction,” said Krisztián Fülöp, Head of Credipass Hungary.

“For these buyers, a market-rate mortgage is not necessarily a prerequisite for purchasing a property, but rather a tool for optimising the financing structure. Because they typically provide a larger down payment, changes in mortgage interest rates have a much smaller impact on transaction activity than they do for buyers relying on subsidised loans.”

Budapest and Pest county still dominates

Geographically, the market for above-average-priced properties remains highly concentrated, with four out of five transactions taking place in Budapest and Pest County. Compared with last year, however, the capital’s share has declined, while Pest County’s has increased.

Demand is increasingly shifting towards the Budapest metropolitan area, where Érd recorded a similar number of transactions to the strongest-performing districts of the capital. Outside the Budapest region, Debrecen and Pécs stand out as the leading markets.

This might interest you: From the offer to the land registry extract — how a safe property purchase works in Hungary

The premium and luxury market operates by different rules

The top end of the market – premium and luxury properties – continues to operate very differently from the mass market.

“Every property worth more than HUF 300 million is unique, which means every transaction is unique as well,” said Tamás Viola, Head of Duna House Prime. “This is not a mass market; success depends on matching the right buyer with the right property.

Pricing itself requires specialist expertise. No two properties are the same, and determining a realistic asking price demands considerable experience. Setting the wrong price can easily add several months to the sales process.”

World.title: Budapest’s new main square moves forward as long-awaited city centre park gets final approval
World.content:
A long-awaited transformation in the heart of Budapest is set to move forward after the capital received the final permit needed to build the new City Hall Park (Városháza Park). The project will replace a former government parking lot with a large public green space, which Mayor Gergely Karácsony says will become Budapest’s “new main square.”

The mayor announced on Tuesday that the Budapest Government Office had issued the heritage protection permit, marking the end of a lengthy approval process and allowing work to progress to the detailed construction planning phase.

Seven years in the making

Karácsony recalled that creating the park was among his earliest campaign promises when he first ran for mayor around seven years ago. At the time, the fenced-off site could only be viewed by climbing a ladder, as the area had long served as a restricted office parking lot with almost no vegetation.

According to the mayor, the project was delayed by years of planning, public consultations, procurement procedures and administrative approvals. He also cited state bureaucracy and the capital’s financial disputes with the previous government as factors that slowed progress.

Before work on the park could begin, the city also had to renovate the deteriorating façade of Budapest City Hall and restore the long-closed Merlin cultural venue, which forms part of the wider redevelopment.

Designed for a changing climate

City Hall Park has been designed with sustainability at its core. The project incorporates a “sponge city” concept aimed at improving rainwater management and helping the space withstand the impacts of climate change.

Plans include approximately 7,730 square metres of green space, 6,966 square metres of rainwater-collecting pavement, and 850 square metres of permeable surfaces. The park will also feature 80 trees planted using the Stockholm planting method, a technique that provides healthier underground conditions for urban trees, allowing them to grow larger and live longer while providing more shade.

The landscaping will also include extensive perennial planting to increase biodiversity and improve the comfort of visitors during increasingly hot summers.

More on the Hungarian capital: 12 surprising American connections in Budapest worth discovering

More than just a park

The development forms part of the broader Open City Hall concept, which aims to make the historic City Hall complex more accessible to residents and visitors.

Plans include opening up the building’s ground floor, renovating the vast Ratskeller space beneath the ceremonial hall, and creating cafés, terraces and hospitality venues that connect directly to the new public square.

Karácsony said the project is intended to create much more than another urban park. Instead, he described City Hall Park as a new civic meeting place that will serve as Budapest’s central public square for decades to come.

World.title: You can run to Revolut, but you can’t hide: Debt collectors can now freeze Hungarian accounts
World.content:
Hungarian debt collectors have begun enforcing collection orders against Revolut accounts after the fintech completed the transfer of its domestic retail customers to its Hungarian branch.

Reports from Hungarian Revolut users indicate that the first account freezes have already been implemented. Customers affected by enforcement proceedings have received notifications from the bank by email and through the application informing them that temporary restrictions have been placed on their accounts due to a seizure order.

Local branch opens the door to enforcement

The development follows Revolut Bank’s recent restructuring of its Hungarian operations. Earlier this month, the company announced that it had successfully transferred more than two million Hungarian retail customers to the newly established Hungarian branch of Revolut Bank UAB.

That move also made it significantly easier for Hungarian judicial enforcement officers to identify and contact the institution when pursuing outstanding debts. According to reports, enforcement officers can now send official requests to the Hungarian branch to determine whether a debtor holds an account with Revolut and, where applicable, initiate an account seizure.

A Hungarian enforcement officer previously confirmed that Revolut Bank’s Hungarian branch had become visible in the domestic enforcement system, enabling authorities to begin using the same collection procedures that apply to traditional banks operating in Hungary.

More on finance: Digital euro? European Parliament’s project is one step closer now

Warning issued years ago

The latest developments do not come as a complete surprise. Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) warned as early as three years ago that taxpayers should not assume money held in Revolut accounts would be beyond the reach of authorities.

At the time, NAV stressed that tax debts could also be collected from Revolut accounts, cautioning against using the platform to shield assets from enforcement, writes Economx.

Now, those warnings have become a practical reality. Users in Revolut community groups have reported receiving messages stating that “temporary restrictions have been applied to your account due to a seizure order,” with enforcement officers confirming that such account freezes have been actively processed in recent weeks.

The change means that Revolut accounts in Hungary are now effectively subject to the same debt collection mechanisms as accounts held with domestic banks, removing what some debtors may have viewed as a financial safe haven.

World.title: Péter Magyar’s first major misstep? What the presidential nomination really revealed
World.content:
Péter Magyar has suffered his first serious political setback, but the controversy over Hungary’s next president was never really about the nominee—it was about how the decision was made.

Only days ago, the Prime Minister appeared to have secured what many saw as a decisive political victory. Following President Tamás Sulyok’s decision to sign the constitutional amendment paving the way for his own removal from office, the government seemed firmly in control of events.

That momentum, however, quickly unravelled.

The government’s preferred candidate for the presidency, chess legend Judit Polgár, announced that she would not accept the nomination, explaining that she did not feel she possessed “the strength required to shoulder the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation.”

Péter Magyar later confirmed that the decision was directly linked to the political climate surrounding the nomination.

“Judit told me that, given the circumstances that had developed, she could not accept the nomination,” he wrote.

So what exactly went wrong?

What were these “circumstances” that triggered such an unusually intense reaction—not only across the political spectrum, but among many of Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s own supporters?

Personnel decisions that initially appeared surprising have hardly been uncommon in recent months. Former Fidesz figures have already been appointed to prominent government positions, while several ministerial nominations have raised eyebrows without generating lasting political damage. Even significant last-minute changes in cabinet appointments have previously passed with relatively little controversy.

Why, then, did the nomination of the next President of Hungary become such a public relations disaster?

The choice of Judit Polgár herself hardly explains the backlash. Internationally respected and widely admired beyond party politics, she possesses precisely the kind of public profile many associate with the largely symbolic office of head of state.

Critics have understandably argued that a constitutional lawyer might have been better equipped to exercise the presidency’s role as an institutional safeguard. Others questioned reports regarding Polgár’s dual citizenship, suggesting that such issues could complicate the office’s constitutional standing.

Yet none of these criticisms alone seem sufficient to explain the thousands of hostile comments that emerged from individuals identifying themselves as supporters of the Tisza movement.

More than a communications failure

In his public response, Prime Minister Péter Magyar acknowledged that communication mistakes had contributed to the controversy and accepted personal responsibility for them.

But the deeper problem appears to lie elsewhere.

The communications errors did not create the political problem—they exposed it.

The sequence of events is revealing.

On Saturday evening, President Tamás Sulyok unexpectedly announced that he would sign the constitutional amendment.

Just over half an hour later, Péter Magyar released a video inviting political parties, civil organisations and ordinary citizens to submit proposals for suitable presidential candidates. The message suggested that, unlike previous political practices, the decision would emerge from public consultation rather than from negotiations behind closed doors.

Then came the surprise.

Barely twenty-four hours later, on Sunday, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that he intended to ask Judit Polgár to serve as the government’s candidate for the presidency.

That single announcement immediately prompted an uncomfortable question among many supporters.

If the decision had already been made, what exactly had the public consultation been for?

Thousands of members of local Tisza groups and many sympathetic voters began asking whether their participation had ever genuinely been intended to influence the outcome.

After all, can a meaningful national consultation really take place within a single weekend?

A decision announced too quickly

The problem may not have been the choice itself.

Indeed, Judit Polgár may well have proved to be an excellent president. Following her withdrawal, however, that possibility will never be tested.

Instead, the political damage resulted from the speed with which the nomination was announced.

Had the government allowed several days—or preferably a week or two—for nominations to be submitted, consultations to take place and discussions with political and civic representatives to unfold publicly, the same decision might well have been received very differently.

The appearance of an open process often matters almost as much as the outcome itself.

Instead, many supporters concluded that the consultation had become little more than a formality.

Péter Magyar has been very patient for more than two years. Why the rush now?

Perhaps the most puzzling aspect of the episode is that there appeared to be no compelling reason for such haste.

Even the constitutional amendment removing the incumbent president did not obviously require completion in the middle of the summer. Its implementation could easily have been delayed until September without any obvious constitutional consequences.

And even once the amendment had been adopted, there was no evident necessity to identify a successor within twenty-four hours.

The accelerated timetable ultimately created problems that a slower process might have avoided entirely.

More on the Hungarian government: Péter Magyar proposes lowering voting age to 16

An opportunity to rebuild trust

Political mistakes are rarely fatal in themselves.

This episode has certainly not become an existential crisis for Péter Magyar or the Tisza movement. Nevertheless, it has highlighted an important expectation among their own supporters.

For months, the movement has promised a different style of governance—one based on transparency, consultation and broader civic participation.

The presidential nomination has raised understandable questions about how those promises will function in practice.

The search for a new presidential candidate now offers an immediate opportunity to demonstrate that public consultation is intended to be more than a political slogan.

If the next process proves genuinely open, inclusive and deliberative, this episode may ultimately be remembered less as a defining failure than as an early lesson in the practical challenges of meeting voters’ expectations.
