World.title: Aleksandre Kartozia to receive accreditation as Georgia’s ambassador to Germany
World.content:
Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

Aleksandre Kartozia, who was appointed Georgia‘s ambassador to Germany in September last year, is set to present his credentials to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on 23 July.

The information was published on the official website of the German president.

The website lists the ambassadorial accreditation ceremonies scheduled for 23 July. Seven ambassadors are due to present their credentials, with Kartozia first on the programme. According to the schedule, his accreditation ceremony is set to begin at 10:30.

Ambassadors from Chile, Honduras, Nigeria, Mauritania, Madagascar and the Vatican’s Apostolic Nuncio are also scheduled to be accredited on the same day.

Why is the accreditation important?

Aleksandre Kartozia was appointed Georgia’s ambassador to Germany in September last year, succeeding Levan Izoria, who had served in the post since 2020.

Before an ambassador can officially take up their duties in Germany, they must present their credentials to the country’s president. Only after this ceremony are they formally accredited and able to carry out the full responsibilities of the role. Until now, Kartozia had been awaiting an invitation to present his credentials.

Letters of credence are official documents by which one head of state appoints a diplomat as their representative to another country.

The documents identify the appointed diplomat and their diplomatic rank. They also contain a formal request from the sending head of state to the receiving head of state to “give credence” to everything the diplomat says or does on behalf of their country.

The accreditation also carries added political significance given the strained relationship between Georgia and Germany.

Relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have been tense over the past two years. Senior Georgian officials have repeatedly criticised Germany’s ambassador to Georgia, Peter Fischer, while Germany has voiced concern over developments in Georgia.

There have also been several occasions when the German ambassador was summoned by the Georgian authorities.

On 31 December 2024, Germany imposed entry bans on nine people it said were responsible for violence against protesters and opposition figures in Georgia.

Who is Aleksandre Kartozia?

Aleksandre Kartozia served as Georgia’s education minister from 1998 to 2004 under President Eduard Shevardnadze.

He has worked as a researcher and taught courses and seminars at leading universities in Berlin, Frankfurt and Bremen. In 2022, he was awarded the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany.

During his tenure as education minister, Kartozia faced corruption allegations. In 2002, Givi Targamadze, a member of Georgia’s Anti-Corruption Council, publicly accused him of corruption. In 2004, prosecutors charged Kartozia and his deputy, Vladimir Sanadze, with abuse of office and the embezzlement of public funds.

Accreditation of Georgia’s ambassador to Germany

World.title: President Aliyev’s visit to Germany: Pragmatism, energy and changing South Caucasus
World.content:
President Aliyev’s visit to Germany

President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan arrived in Berlin on Sunday evening for an official visit. An official welcoming ceremony was held at Berlin Brandenburg Airport, where the Azerbaijani leader also met Michael Harms, chairman of the German Eastern Business Association.

As the visit has only just begun, few details have emerged about its outcomes. However, information released so far, together with the broader context, suggests the trip could mark a new phase in relations between Baku and Berlin, driven by pragmatism, closer economic cooperation and a shared interest in regional stability.

What is known so far?

According to official information, Aliyev’s meeting with Michael Harms highlighted growing interest among Azerbaijani and German businesses in expanding cooperation. The two sides also discussed ways to institutionalise that cooperation. They exchanged views on opportunities in both conventional and renewable energy, as well as on developing transport, logistics and communications links, including the Middle Corridor.

Officials also noted that Azerbaijan has adopted a new state programme for agriculture. The two sides discussed the potential for introducing German technologies, particularly in the field of smart farming. Tourism development and other issues of mutual interest were also on the agenda.

The groundwork for the visit had been laid well before Aliyev arrived in Berlin. On 4 December 2025, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called President Aliyev to congratulate him on progress in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. He reaffirmed Germany’s support for regional stability and invited the Azerbaijani leader to visit Germany. Aliyev accepted the invitation and, in turn, invited the chancellor to visit Azerbaijan.

On 15 June 2026, Germany’s ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ralf Horlemann, said during a farewell meeting that the visit was expected to take place later in the year.

Bilateral trade reached around €1.7 billion in 2025, while more than 250 German companies operate in Azerbaijan. Since the beginning of 2026, Azerbaijan has also started direct gas exports to Germany and Austria. These figures, together with recent economic initiatives, underline the visit’s strong commercial focus.

The broader trajectory of bilateral relations is also noteworthy. In April 2025, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier paid an official visit to Azerbaijan—the first official visit by a German head of state to the country. Aliyev, for his part, has travelled to Germany on several occasions to attend the Munich Security Conference and other international events.

Why is this visit taking place?

The visit reinforces the pragmatic nature of relations between Azerbaijan and Germany, which are increasingly centred on expanding economic cooperation. As Europe continues to diversify its energy supplies and reduce its dependence on Russian gas, Azerbaijan has strengthened its position as a reliable and predictable energy supplier.

The start of direct gas exports to Germany and Austria in 2026 marked a significant step in that process. But the visit’s agenda extends beyond energy. Discussions are expected to focus on a broader “energy-plus” framework, encompassing cooperation in logistics, the Middle Corridor, industry, agricultural technology and tourism. German businesses, supported by the German Eastern Business Association, have shown growing interest in these sectors.

Germany also attaches considerable importance to stability in the South Caucasus, particularly the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. This was reflected in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s phone call with President Aliyev in December 2025, during which he highlighted the importance of the peace agenda. From Berlin’s perspective, Azerbaijan’s multi-vector foreign policy has therefore taken on additional significance, with Baku seen both as an energy supplier and as a participant in efforts to strengthen regional stability.

The Berlin visit also comes against the backdrop of growing tensions between Azerbaijan and the Council of Europe, following President Aliyev’s remarks at the Shusha Global Media Forum that the country could fully withdraw from the organisation. In that sense, the trip highlights the tension between Europe’s values-based agenda and its pragmatic interests. At the same time, current developments suggest that relations between Germany and Azerbaijan continue to be shaped primarily by economic interests and a shared commitment to regional stability.

Europe’s approach to Azerbaijan remains far from uniform. While some European institutions have taken a critical stance towards Baku, bilateral relations with individual partners continue to be driven largely by pragmatic considerations. This reflects Azerbaijan’s continued pursuit of a selective and multi-vector foreign policy.

What outcomes can be expected?

As the visit has only just begun, few official details have been released. Even so, the main areas of cooperation are already becoming clear. One of the central themes of Aliyev’s meeting with Michael Harms was the institutionalisation of business ties, including the creation of new mechanisms for cooperation, business councils and joint working groups.

Among the most likely outcomes are progress in talks on increasing energy exports, broader involvement of German companies in Middle Corridor projects, greater technology transfer and investment in agriculture, as well as new joint initiatives in tourism.

Meetings with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, other senior government officials and representatives of the German business community are also expected to take place during the visit. The agenda may include the signing of cooperation agreements and the adoption of roadmaps for future collaboration.

The longer-term outlook extends well beyond the immediate visit. Both sides are seeking to diversify Azerbaijan’s ties with Europe, expand investment, strengthen the Middle Corridor’s role in Eurasian logistics and increase bilateral trade, which currently stands at €1.7 billion. At the same time, risks remain. Future cooperation could be affected by fluctuations in energy prices, differing approaches among European governments towards Azerbaijan and the overall stability of the South Caucasus.

The visit therefore reflects the pragmatic and multi-vector nature of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy. Baku is seeking to move beyond its role as an energy supplier and position itself as a broader economic and logistics partner. Berlin, for its part, has an interest in strengthening cooperation with a reliable partner while supporting stability in the South Caucasus. The full results of the visit will become clearer in the coming days, but it is already evident that relations are evolving towards an “energy-plus” partnership from which both sides expect tangible economic benefits.

President Aliyev’s visit to Germany

World.title: ‘Police violence in Georgia has become part of everyday life,’ says Social Justice Center
World.content:
Police violence in Georgia

According to the Social Justice Center, physical violence, ill-treatment and abuse of power by law enforcement officers in Georgia have gone beyond isolated cases of police misconduct and become a routine feature of the system.

The organisation says recent information points to the normalisation of inhuman treatment of detainees, describing the trend as deeply alarming.

The organisation says police violence is driven by several factors, including a lack of political will, weak institutional oversight, a culture of impunity and political influence over the police.

It argues that the cases reported by the media represent only a fraction of the true scale of the violence.

According to the organisation, most victims choose not to speak out against law enforcement for fear of retaliation, fabricated evidence, new criminal charges or being falsely accused of drug offences.

High-profile cases: Torture, coma and death

The Social Justice Center highlights several serious cases that have recently received widespread media attention.

The case of Alan Kakitashvili and Irakli Tatunashvili

Friends Alan Kakitashvili and Irakli Tatunashvili were arrested at a police station in Tbilisi last year following a fight at a restaurant in the city of Gori.

Kakitashvili says that he and Tatunashvili were severely beaten inside the police station. After being questioned at the Gldani-Nadzaladevi police station, Tatunashvili was taken to hospital in a coma. He died on 9 June 2025.

Alan Kakitashvili himself spent nine months in prison before being fully acquitted by two courts.

Although an investigation into the alleged police violence has been launched, Tatunashvili has yet to be granted victim status and has not been questioned by investigators.

Violence at Dusheti police station

The Georgian broadcaster Pirveli recently aired a report in which Aleksandre Gogochuri said he had been beaten by around 15 employees of the Dusheti municipal administration.

According to the Social Justice Center, prosecutors dropped the criminal investigation against the alleged perpetrator but instead charged Gogochuri with giving false testimony, avoiding the question of possible police accountability.

Gori: Dozens of police officers accused of assaulting two men

On 27 May 2026, the news outlet Kartlis Ambebi published video footage appearing to show more than 10 police officers beating two men.

These are only a small number of the high-profile cases reported in recent months.

The Social Justice Center says it has documented hundreds of cases of violence during the dispersal of protests and the arrest of demonstrators over the past two years.

The organisation also cites findings by the Public Defender, which indicate that the number of people reporting ill-treatment after arrest has continued to rise.

According to the report, 30.2% of those detained during the 20–21 June 2019 protests said they had been subjected to ill-treatment. That figure rose to 79.5% among those detained between 29 November and 2 December 2024, and to 88% for arrests made between 2 and 3 February 2025.

Despite the scale of the violence, the organisation says no adequate legal response has been taken to date.

What needs to change?

The Social Justice Center says preventing police violence requires:

Independent and impartial investigations into alleged crimes committed by police officers that are timely, effective and unbiased;

into alleged crimes committed by police officers that are timely, effective and unbiased; Appropriate legal classification of ill-treatment under the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, rather than general offences related to abuse of office;

World.title: 'Not finished': Trump signals US strikes on Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site
World.content:
Donald Trump says the US is "not finished" attacking Iran and warns American forces could target Pickaxe Mountain, near Iran's heavily damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility, "pretty soon".

The US president spoke to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, local time, as Tehran continued to step up its strikes across the Middle East.

Pickaxe Mountain is a deeply buried nuclear site near Natanz where Western intelligence suspects Iran is building an undeclared enrichment facility.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Mr Trump said, adding that he would not normally announce targets but "there's not a thing they can do about it".

The US leader projected that it would take the Islamic republic more than 20 years to rebuild from damage sustained in the Middle East war, two weeks after fighting between the decades-old foes resumed.

"If we left right now, it would take Iran 20, 25 years to rebuild," he said. "We're not finished at all... we're not leaving right now."

A satellite view shows tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, of the Natanz nuclear facility, in Iran. (Reuters )

His comments came after Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain came under attack Tuesday.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels meanwhile said they would blockade Saudi Arabia's ports, threatening to throw energy markets into chaos after Iran's Strait of Hormuz blockade.

Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian attacks as sirens sounded multiple times in the kingdom, with Kuwait and Jordan also announcing they had intercepted drone and missile strikes.

Kuwait has said that Tehran hit multiple power and water desalination plants across the country over the past days, including on Monday, forcing residents to ration energy consumption.

Iran's Guards confirmed a strike on Jordan, claiming they had targeted a "complex housing US terrorist forces in the region of Rukban".

The Iranian army had earlier said it targeted US assets in Kuwait and Bahrain, including air defence systems, radar installations and administrative buildings.

"With this radar sweep, the enemy should prepare for even more decisive and powerful waves of drone and missile attacks," the Guards said in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA.

Houthi threat

US President Donald Trump said US forces would "take care of" the Houthi rebels if the Iran-backed militant group followed through on its threatened blockade of Saudi ports.

"If something like that happens, we take care of it," Mr Trump said.

"You know, we've done that with the Houthis before, and we haven't heard from them in a while since we did what we did originally."

Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the threat from what it called the "terrorist Houthi militia" and said it "continues to support the brotherly Yemeni people and their legitimate government".

It remains unclear how the Houthis would implement their blockade of Saudi ports, and oil markets eased slightly despite the threat from Iran's ally against the world's biggest crude exporter.

Houthis declare maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia In a statement, the Houthis' military spokesperson Yahya Saree says the group will enforce the blockade against its "criminal Saudi enemy", effective immediately.

But maritime intelligence provider Vanguard Tech said a Singapore-flagged tanker and a Liberia-flagged tanker both "reversed course" in the Red Sea after loading crude at the Saudi port of Yanbu following the Houthi warning.

Should the Houthis make good on their threat to blockade Saudi ports, that would put at risk Riyadh's ability to bypass Hormuz for some of its oil exports and have major repercussions for the global economy.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis traded fire last week for the first time in years, threatening a 2022 truce in their years-long conflict, but the rebels have largely remained on the sidelines since Israel and the US attacked Iran in late February.

The Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that two tankers attempting to transit Hormuz "were hit by explosions, resulting in massive fires that brought them to a standstill".

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) earlier reported that an "unknown projectile" struck a tanker off the coast of Oman.

Following the deaths of at least three US soldiers in recent days, the US launched a new round of attacks against Iran on Monday it said was "designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping" in the Strait of Hormuz.

The deaths bring to 17 the number of fatalities among US service members. Nearly 100 US service members have been wounded since war resumed on July 7, the Pentagon said Monday.

Trump promises US help for Lebanon

President Donald Trump met with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House in Washington on Tuesday. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

Mr Trump met with Joseph Aoun in Washington on Tuesday as the Lebanese president sought US backing to disarm Hezbollah and forge a path to peace with Israel.

Meeting Mr Aoun at the White House, Mr Trump said Lebanon had been "a very mistreated country" that had been "hit hard" for decades.

"It's probably a dangerous place in a lot of ways," Mr Trump told reporters.

" But they love the country ... and we're going to help it. We're going to help it a lot. "

The first Lebanese president invited to Washington since 2009, Mr Aoun asked Mr Trump for support for the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF), which has begun deploying in southern areas of the country under a US-backed framework agreement with Israel.

The deployment aims at proving Beirut can extend state authority and disarm Iran-backed Hezbollah, which Israel has set as a precondition for ending its occupation in southern Lebanon.

But in a sign of the fragility of the agreement, the Lebanese army said Israeli troops fired near its soldiers deploying in a so-called "pilot zone" Israel is supposed to withdraw from.

These "pilot zones" are primarily located just outside territory that Israeli forces invaded after Hezbollah opened rocket fire on Israel and drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had only fired "warning shots into the air" after Lebanese soldiers entered an area that was "not part of the pilot area."

Asked whether Washington would put additional pressure on Israel to withdraw, Mr Trump said: "We'll be looking at that."

AP/AFP

World.title: UK politician Ann Widdecombe hit 21 times with hammer, prosecutors allege
World.content:
Former British politician Ann Widdecombe was struck 21 times on the head with a hammer as she was eating lunch at home, a prosecutor told a court hearing on Tuesday, local time, for the man charged in her murder.

Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in London over the killing that shocked the public and the political establishment.

Ms Widdecombe, 78, was eating around noon on July 8 when Kerry drove to her house in an isolated south-west England village, prosecutor Kashif Malik said.

Mr Kerry walked through the front door and beat her with a hammer, took her wallet and was gone two minutes after the attack began.

Blunt force injury to the head was listed as the provisional cause of death.

Joshua Kerry, 28, appears at Westminster Magistrates' Court for the first time since being charged over Ann Widdecombe's death. (AP: Elizabeth Cook/PA)

Mr Kerry was charged on Monday afternoon, local time, while in custody after being arrested on suspicion of murder and acts of terror.

Police are investigating his motive, including a potential political or terrorist connection, prosecutors said.

Mr Kerry, who wore a gray sweatsuit, spoke only to confirm his identity and did not enter a plea. He was ordered held in custody and is scheduled to appear in the Central Criminal Court on Oct. 9.

Ms Widdecombe, a former member of parliament and government minister, was a prominent political voice known for her blunt-spoken, socially conservative views opposing abortion and the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.

When she failed to appear for a scheduled interview on July 8, TV producers called her assistant, who contacted her gardener, prosecutors said. He found Ms Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor the next day.

Mr Kerry was arrested July 11 in South Yorkshire, a northern English county where he lived, more than 400 kilometres from Ms Widdecombe's home in the village of Haytor, on the edge of Dartmoor National Park.

Prosecutors allege Ann Widdecombe was attacked as she was having lunch on July 8. (AP: Matt Keeble/PA )

Ms Widdecombe was a MP in the House of Commons from 1987 to 2010, serving as a prisons minister in Prime Minister John Major's 1990s Conservative government.

She found fame after leaving Parliament as a contestant on the reality television shows "Strictly Come Dancing" and "Celebrity Big Brother."

She later joined the Brexit Party, briefly serving as a member of the European Parliament before Britain left the European Union in 2020.

Most recently, she joined the anti-immigration Reform UK, often appearing in the media as the party's immigration and justice spokesperson.

Ms Widdecombe's killing has renewed concerns over the security for politicians, which had been tightened in the past decade after the murders of two prominent MPs.

Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.

AP

World.title: 'Irresponsible': Russia conducts live-fire weapons exercise off British coast
World.content:
A Russian naval ship carried out a live-fire weapons exercise in international waters off southern England, Britain's defence ministry says.

The ship, in the Channel around 40 miles (74 km) south of the UK port of Plymouth, on Monday, local time, informed a British naval patrol vessel, HMS Tyne, of its intention to fire and asked it to move to a safer position, the ministry said.

"The exercise was subsequently carried out in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes."

The British Navy monitored the exercise and was continuing to track the vessel closely, the ministry added.

Newly-appointed UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting described the incident as "performative and irresponsible", at a press conference in London.

Wes Streeting is the United Kingdom's new defence minister. (AP: Kirsty Gigglesworth)

"Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government and this prime minister, our resolve to stand against Russian aggression in Ukraine but also Russian aggression against all of our allies," he added.

British media named the ship as the Neustrashimy, a frigate in Russia's Baltic Fleet, noting the incident happened on the first day in office of Britain's new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham.

In June, a Russian warship fired warning shots to a yacht in the English Channel.

Russia said that boat was on a dangerous course and Britain's defence ministry downplayed the incident at the time, insisting it was an "isolated" event "to prevent a possible collision".

Russian warships are reportedly being used to escort tankers through the Channel that are associated with Russia's "shadow fleet" of sanctions-breaking ships.

Last month, around the time of the yacht incident, British armed forces intercepted a sanctioned Russian tanker in the first such UK-led operation.

AFP

World.title: Protests turn violent after man dies during Italian police arrest
World.content:
Human rights campaigners and Italy's opposition parties are demanding answers after a man died under police restraint as he pleaded for help, while government leaders defended the police.

The incident has been likened to George Floyd's murder in the United States six years ago, and also prompted comparisons with tactics used by the US's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) under President Donald Trump.

Abderrahim Fakir, a 42-year-old from Morocco who moved to Italy when he was five, died on Sunday, local time, in Bologna while being forcibly held down by two police officers, according to a video shared widely on Italian media.

On Tuesday, after anti-police protests turned violent and left dozens of officers injured, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for a full investigation into the death.

At least 56 officers were injured in clashes with protesters after the death. (Reuters: Michele Lapini)

But Ms Meloni also criticised the protests in the aftermath which turned violent and left 56 officers injured, according to Italy's police union.

"Those who chose to use this incident as a pretext to lay waste to the city, attack officers and spread violence ... were not seeking the truth: they were seeking confrontation," Ms Meloni said.

In the video, Mr Fakir -- who reportedly suffered from heart issues and asthma -- repeatedly calls out "aiuto, aiuto, basta" ("help, help, that's enough") as the officers sit on him and ambulance workers look on.

After he stops moving, the police bind his ankles together.

Only after a moment or two do they and the ambulance workers check his vital signs, the video shows.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says she wants to see a full investigation into the police's actions. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

Called to the scene by local residents concerned by Mr Fakir's erratic behaviour, the police officers had told the ambulance personnel that he was "having a psychiatric episode", according to media reports.

"You can't die like this," Mr Fakir's sister Khadija told the Corriere della Sera daily.

"The police have to protect us. If someone is agitated, you have to calm them down... not kill them like a dog," she said.

Prosecutors in Bologna have opened a probe and have requested the officers' body cam footage.

'Inhumane'

The incident triggered a protest in Bologna on Monday in which participants, according to images posted on social media, held up slogans such as "Justice and truth for Fakir!" and "State murderers".

Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi told state television network Rai1: "Whoever makes insulting remarks against the police shows they have no trust in our law enforcement nor in our justice system (and) should look into what happened."

Italy's far-right Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini also defended the police, while Galeazzo Bignami, head of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Brothers of Italy party in parliament's lower house, praised the officers' "professional conduct".

Protesters took to the streets of Bologna calling for "Justice for Fakir". (Reuters: Michele Lapini)

But Senator Ilaria Cucchi, whose brother died in custody in 2009, told AFP she was sickened by the "solidarity and thanks" expressed to police after such an "inhumane act".

Ms Cucchi, a member of the opposition Greens and Left alliance (AVS) party, slammed Ms Meloni and her right-wing coalition government, saying their "policies seeped in hatred and racism" have fostered a climate of violence.

Francesco Boccia, head of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD) in the Senate, told the Repubblica daily that "if the right wants to import the ICE model, this is the wrong country for it. We have democratic antibodies".

Lawyer Barbara Spinelli told the ANSA news agency that she had met Fakir last year, when he applied to renew his permit to stay.

He was "a very kind, well educated, respectful person" who was in Italy legally, but who worried about being expelled.

"I told him: 'We are in Italy, a democratic country. Here the police respect the rules'," she said.

"I don't know how I will ever again manage to tell someone they don't need to be afraid", she added.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: AI companies 'stole' Australian culture, news bosses say as they call for licensing deals
World.content:
The heads of Australia's biggest media companies have demanded that AI companies pay for the "public good" of Australian news and culture used without permission to train their technology.

Australian news agencies are already in talks for licensing deals, with the ABC's chief revealing that AI developer Anthropic had approached it about audio and video that capture how Australians speak.

The comments came during a panel featuring the heads of the ABC, SBS, Nine and News Corp Australasia at the annual Andrew Olle lecture on Tuesday night.

The wide-ranging discussion covered everything from the role of AI in journalism to new detail about the departure of former Today show host Karl Stefanovic.

ABC chief reveals AI firm Anthropic approached the broadcaster seeking audio and video of Australians speaking. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

ABC managing director Hugh Marks told the audience that journalism was a public good that needed to be protected.

"If we lose sight of the work that's being done … then I think we'll have a worse nation," he said.

Mr Marks argued that AI companies should strike deals with Australian news companies to license works, but also acknowledged a "delicate balance" with also providing high-quality information to Australians who are using AI.

This obligation to inform shouldn't mean that news organisations should be expected to let AI companies train on news free of charge, SBS managing director Jane Palfreyman said: "Our collective view on that would be no."

Hugh Marks says AI developers should pay Australian news organisations to license their content. (ABC News: John Gunn)

News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller said that AI companies knew that the "theft" of Australian works was a "risk to their business in Australia".

Nine chief executive and managing director Matt Stanton said his company's recent licensing deal, under which its journalism will be cited in answers from Microsoft's AI tool Copilot, was a "good deal for both sides".

Mr Stanton said that Nine's decision to cut 30 job was not "directly" as a result of AI, when pressed by panel moderator ABC Radio Sydney Mornings host Hamish Macdonald.

He also said Karl Stefanovic's "different directions" of his podcast had prompted Nine's decision to part ways with the former Today host, even before his controversial podcast with Tommy Robinson.

Paying for journalism

The panel discussion followed a lecture by global news agency Reuters' editor-in-chief Alessandra Galloni, who urged news organisations to set firm terms for artificial intelligence companies using their work and to share what they learn when AI tools go wrong.

How journalism can stay relevant in the AI age What will a trusted, sustainable, global news organisation look like in an era of agentic AI?

Ms Galloni said journalism remains the source of reliable, first-hand reporting on which people and increasingly AI systems depend.

She cited recent research showing that 10 per cent of people access chatbots for news each week, including 16 per cent of people under 35.

Ms Galloni argued publishers had no reason to give up on reaching those audience but should strike deals to have their journalism correctly attributed, accurately represented and paid for by the AI companies.

"Our journalism should be licensed, not taken," she said.

She cited a speech delivered by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week where he promised that Australian writers, musicians, artists and journalists would retain control over work used to build and train AI.

Using AI in the newsroom

Ms Galloni argued that it is the responsibility of news organisations to help society understand the "pitfalls and possibilities of AI."

She said that Reuters using AI to help reporters search large collections of documents, find patterns and turn official material into fast news updates, summaries and translations.

She cited investigations that used AI to document thousands of social media posts and speeches by US President Donald Trump, and to convert 20,000 pages of Syrian government documents into searchable text that was used in an investigation that uncovered a mass grave.

Experts, union warn about ABC's AI use Experts and the journalists’ union have welcomed the ABC’s plans to use artificial intelligence responsibly, but warned misuse could damage trust in the public broadcaster.

Reuters is also using AI to produce headlines from press releases, draft first paragraphs in urgent stories, generate bullet-point summaries and translate stories, Ms Galloni said.

But Reuters only published journalism produced with AI once it had been reviewed by a journalist and its use was disclosed when it played a significant role in what was published, she said.

She said on top of the AI's struggles with providing nuance and context, it is also vulnerable to hallucinations and other mistakes. One third-party tool tested by Reuters had once mistaken a SpaceX spacecraft for a missile, she said.

"Thankfully we caught it," she said.

Ms Galloni said even advances in AI could not replace the reporting that made news valuable in the first place.

Reuters has 2,600 journalists in 165 countries, she said, including 70 staff covering the war in Ukraine and Russia.

"In my conversations with tech companies, I have often been struck by how little they understand about what original, first-hand, on-the-ground journalism is and looks like," she said

Sharing what works

Ms Galloni called on rival news organisations to share the lessons emerging from those experiments, drawing a comparison to the way that competing journalists will exchange safety information when in war zones.

"I would venture that it is our collective responsibility — to the public, to society — to enhance our and their understanding about the pitfalls and possibilities of AI," she said.

The Andrew Olle media lecture was first held in 1996 to honour the ABC radio and television broadcaster who died from an undiagnosed brain tumour in 1995.

Each year's lecture features a speech on the future of journalism in Australia and raises funds for charity Brain Cancer Australia.

Previous lecturers have included New York Times executive editor Joseph Kahn, Ray Martin and former News Corp co-chairman Lachlan Murdoch as well as ABC journalists Leigh Sales and Fran Kelly.

World.title: Inquest to determine whether man killed his mother and staged her death
World.content:
Warning: This article contains references to mental health and suicide. It also contains details readers may find distressing.

An inquest is being held to determine whether a man killed his mother before placing her in the driver's seat of her car to stage that she was behind the wheel during a crash.

Tracee Ann Grosvenor, 58, and her son Ethan Grosvenor, 27, crashed into a tree on Langhorne Creek Road, about 60 kilometres south-east of Adelaide, on December 3, 2022.

Opening the inquest in South Australia's Coroners Court today, counsel assisting the coroner Darren Evans said the court would ask Deputy State Coroner Naomi Kereru to determine if Mr Grosvenor killed his mother.

Mr Evans said the court would also seek to determine whether "safety issues" had been identified and addressed after Mr Grosvenor took his own life 11 days later.

He told the court Mrs Grosvenor was in the driver's seat when police arrived at the crash scene early on December 4, but that DNA evidence later showed her body had been moved.

"Her lower legs and body were in the driver's side, with her upper body lying across the centre console into the passenger side," Mr Evans said.

"Members of SAPOL's Major Crash Section formed the view that the injuries Mrs Grovsenor had sustained were inconsistent with the dynamics of the collision if she was seated in the driver's seat.

"DNA evidence subsequently effectively confirmed that Mr Grosvenor was driving the car at the time [of the collision] and that after [it] he had picked Mrs Grovsenor up over his shoulder and put her into the driver's seat."

Tracee Ann Grosvenor died in December 2022. (Supplied)

Mr Evans also said that, after the crash, an "independent witness" came forward and said she had seen the same car pulled over by the side of the road about 10:30pm on December 3 and that "Mrs Grosvenor was in the passenger seat, appearing distressed".

Mr Grosvenor sustained minor injuries in the accident and was detained under the Mental Health Act.

The act gives South Australian doctors the power to lawfully treat and, in certain cases, detain people affected by mental illness.

Son died days after crash

Mr Evans told the court that Mr Grosvenor took his own life on December 14, 2022, after leaving the waiting room of the Adelaide Dental Hospital on North Terrace in the CBD.

The inquest heard that Mr Grosvenor was supervised by his occupational therapist, Rachael Rolla, at the appointment because he was at "risk of absconding".

Naomi Kereru will hand down her findings later. (ABC News)

Ms Rolla told the court the 27-year-old "asked to go to the toilet" and never returned.

"There was no policy at the time to indicate what to do if someone had asked to go to the toilet," she said.

Ms Rolla said she was aware Mr Grosvenor had gone missing from the Adelaide Dental Hospital days earlier on December 9, 2022, while being supervised by registered nurse Jennifer Williams.

"At that point, did you consider: 'Well, I know that he went missing before in this building, I really should pay particularly close attention to where he is about to go?'" Mr Evans asked.

Ms Rolla responded: "I didn't think it was appropriate to follow a male to the toilet."

The inquest heard that, since Mr Grosvenor's death, changes had been made to the "protocols and procedures" that "governed" mental health patient trips into the community.

Julie Chapman hopes the inquest provides answers. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

Outside the Coroners Court today, Mrs Grosvenor's sister, Julie Chapman, said she hopes the inquest can help achieve justice.

"The system has failed us. We feel like we've just fallen through the cracks," she said.

Ms Chapman said Mr Grosvenor had a history of mental health challenges and had displayed violent behaviour towards his mother, but said mental health services had failed to intervene.

"We need mental health to be taken seriously; we need families to be listened to," she said.

Ms Kereru will deliver her findings at a later date.

World.title: Officer handcuffed teen in lead-up to police station rape, court told
World.content:
A former NSW Police officer accused of raping a 17-year-old girl at the station where he worked "locked up" and "handcuffed" her on two separate occasions months before to the alleged assault, a court has heard.

David Robert Blackbourne was serving as a police officer when he allegedly raped the teenage girl in a NSW-Victoria border town in October, 1998.

He has been charged with two counts of assault with act of indecency, two counts of sexual intercourse without consent, and one count of holder of public office misconduct him or himself.

Mr Blackbourne, 56, was arrested in 2023 and has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

His trial began this week in Sydney's Downing Centre District Court, where the complainant took the witness stand on Tuesday.

She told the court that the accused locked her in a cell months before the alleged rape.

She said she and a friend were picked up by Mr Blackbourne and another officer in a NSW Police vehicle late at night and driven to the station.

"We were told they kept drinks that were confiscated from when they were working and they were kept in a fridge in the police station," the complainant said.

The woman told the court she was offered an alcoholic beverage and that shortly after Mr Blackbourne asked her whether she wanted to see inside one of the cells.

She said yes and walked down the corridor to the cells, the court heard.

"It was a big brick cell and it was very cold and dark and damp," the woman said.

" I went inside and that is when Dave locked me in the cell. "

She said told the court she was in the cell for approximately 10 minutes before Mr Blackbourne unlocked the door.

"I became quite panicked. It was cold and dark," she said.

'Put handcuffs on me'

The complainant told the court that about five weeks later Mr Blackbourne picked her up with a friend and drove them into bushland.

"He stopped the police car and then another police car entered into bushland," she said.

The complainant told the court that David Blackbourne handcuffed her in a police vehicle. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

The woman said a second police officer entered the vehicle and sat in the back seat next to her friend.

"I was in the front seat with Dave and that is when Dave put handcuffs on me," she said.

"He then kissed me."

The Crown prosecutor asked the victim whether she gave Mr Blackbourne permission.

"No I did not," she said.

'He wasn't in a good mood'

The woman told the court that in October 1998 she attended a police station and Mr Blackbourne gave her a police hat that was to be worn at a year 12 muck-up day.

"I walked into the police station and I remember we had a very brief conversation … he wasn't in a good mood," she said.

The woman said Mr Blacbourne gave her the hat near the front counter, but "things changed very quickly".

"He said, 'You are not leaving yet,'" the complainant told the court.

"He then kissed me."

She told the jury she was taken behind the counter and that Mr Blackbourne pulled her pants down and raped her.

She said he then took her to another room and sexually assaulted her again.

"I felt like I was trapped in there," the woman told the court.

She said she left the police station after the alleged assaults and walked home.

She said she was very upset and overwhelmed and stopped on a bridge on the way to her house.

"I was contemplating jumping off [the bridge]," the woman said.

She told the court that the first person she told about the alleged incident was her now-husband in 2002.

The woman contacted Victoria Police in 2016 and the investigation was handed to NSW Police in 2021.

The trial, presided over by Judge Huw Baker SC, continues.

World.title: Five teens plead guilty over deadly train station ambush
World.content:
Five teenagers have admitted to their roles in luring and violently ambushing a man with an acquired brain injury to a New South Wales train station under the pretence he would have sex with a 13-year-old girl.

The four boys and one girl, who were aged between 13 and 15 when Jack Westren was fatally stabbed, pleaded guilty to manslaughter at Port Kembla Children's Court on Tuesday.

Mr Westren, who suffered a brain injury in a motor vehicle accident in 2008, died near Shellharbour Junction train station after being assaulted on January 28 last year.

Court documents state Mr Westren's medical issues manifested in various ways, including messaging girls on social media and asking them inappropriate questions.

His intellectual functioning was assessed to be in the "extremely low" range.

The five teenagers admitted to their involvement in Jack Westren's death. (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

According to court documents, Mr Westren asked someone on Snapchat to give him a girl's phone number on the day of the attack.

That person gave him the number of a 13-year-old boy but said it belonged to "Amy".

Mr Westren began messaging that number, saying, "Do you have a boyfriend yes or no?"

The pair exchanged messages that discussed meeting up to have sex. The boy told Mr Westren him throughout the night "I want you" and "I like older boys".

Flowers were left at the station after Jack Westren's death. (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

Girl used as 'bait'

Court documents show the boy then shared screenshots of the messages exchanged between Mr Westren and "Amy" with his friends.

"There's a paedophile that we're trying to get to come to Shelly tomorrow youse want to bash him?" one message in the group chat said.

Video taken that night showed some of the boys in a front yard, wearing balaclavas and "simulating assaults, kidnapping and robberies with weapons", according to the documents.

The next day Mr Westren asked "Amy" what train she was going to catch to Shellharbour.

The boy and three friends, including a 13-year-old girl who would act as "bait", boarded a train to meet him while the boy continued to exchange messages with Mr Westren.

Jack Westren was fatally attacked after being lured to the station. (Supplied: Simone Westren)

"You are with three boys. I saw you but you just didn't see me," Mr Westren said in a message while he was on the train.

" Have you got people waiting to bash me? "

Another group was waiting in Shellharbour, with some discussing in a group chat that they "were going to bring machetes".

Tamara Doust, 39, allegedly received a message from one of the boys that said, "Wanna come up Shelly? The boys are having a fight".

"Yeah G, what time?" she allegedly replied.

Ms Doust allegedly drove some of the boys to the mall, where they met up with the rest of the group and played games at Timezone before going to Shellharbour Junction.

She allegedly took 11 teenagers to the station, six of whom travelled in the boot.

In a video recording taken by the girl in the boot, one of the boys could be seen wearing a knuckleduster and saying "imagine this hitting him".

Jack Westren believed he was going to meet a girl he met online before he was fatally stabbed. (Supplied: Simone Westren)

'What we did was good'

Court documents state that the ambush that followed was recorded by the girl on her mobile phone.

Ms Doust allegedly ran towards Mr Westren, hit him in the head and called him a "paedo".

He fell to the ground before the teenagers repeatedly kicked and punched him. One allegedly stabbed him in the heart and liver before they all fled back to the car.

People nearby ran to Mr Westren's aid and administered CPR until an ambulance arrived, but he died at the scene.

Some of the teenagers subsequently discussed the incident on social media before their arrest.

"What we did was good," one of the boys said on Snapchat.

The teenagers who faced court today had a charge of murder withdrawn due to their guilty plea to manslaughter.

Court documents stated all were liable for manslaughter on the basis that they agreed to attack Mr Westren as a group in a situation involving dangerous weapons and would have foreseen "an appreciable risk of serious injury".

Ms Doust, who is yet to enter pleas to a charge of murder, will face Wollongong Local Court on Wednesday.

A sixth teenager, a 15-year-old boy, will face the children's court next week.

He is yet to enter a plea to the charge of murder.

London: Former British politician Ann Widdecombe was struck 21 times on the head with a hammer as she was eating lunch at home, a prosecutor told a court hearing on Tuesday for the man charged in her murder. Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court in London over the killing that shocked the public and the political establishment. Widdecombe, 78, was eating around midday on July 8 when Kerry drove to her house in an isolated southwest England village, prosecutor Kashif Malik said. A court artist sketch of accused Joshua Kerry. Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP Kerry walked through the front door and beat her with a hammer, took her wallet and was gone two minutes after the attack began.



Blunt force injury to the head was listed as the provisional cause of death. Kerry was charged on Monday (London time) while in custody after being arrested on suspicion of murder and acts of terror. Police are investigating his motive, including a potential political or terrorist connection, prosecutors said. Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home on July 9. AP Kerry, who wore a grey sweatsuit, spoke only to confirm his identity and did not enter a plea. He was ordered to be held in custody and is scheduled to appear in the Central Criminal Court on October 9. Widdecombe, a former member of Parliament and government minister, was a prominent political voice known for her blunt-spoken, socially conservative views opposing abortion and the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.



When she failed to appear for a scheduled interview on July 8, television producers called her assistant, who contacted her gardener, prosecutors said. He found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor the next day. Kerry was arrested on July 11 in South Yorkshire, a northern England county where he lived, more than 400 kilometres from Widdecombe’s home in the village of Haytor, on the edge of Dartmoor National Park. Loading Widdecombe was a MP in the House of Commons from 1987 to 2010, serving as a prisons minister in Prime Minister John Major’s 1990s Conservative government. She found fame after leaving Parliament as a contestant on the reality television shows Strictly Come Dancing and Celebrity Big Brother.



She later joined the Brexit Party, briefly serving as a member of the European Parliament before Britain left the European Union in 2020. Most recently, she joined the anti-immigration Reform UK, often appearing in the media as the party’s immigration and justice spokesperson. Widdecombe’s killing has renewed concerns over the security for politicians, which had been tightened in the past decade after the murders of two prominent MPs. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
